#4882. Crypto on notice as hawkish Fed risks December ‘meltdown’

Economist Robin Brooks warned of dire consequences for stocks if the Federal Reserve fails to deliver dovish cues before the FOMC blackout period.

Risk assets could face a “full meltdown” within the next two weeks if the US Federal Reserve maintains its hawkish policy outlook, analysis warns.

Economist Robin Brooks, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and former chief foreign exchange (FX) strategist at Goldman Sachs, forecast Wednesday that the US central bank could ultimately abandon its widely expected 25-basis-point interest rate hike in December.

Despite falling oil prices and US dollar strength rising, the Fed has maintained a hawkish stance on future policy moves, signaling that interest rates may need to rise and remain elevated.

Last week, Federal Reserve Gov. Christopher Waller said that the central bank may need to “shock” markets with a 50-basis-point rate hike to curb price increases being passed on to consumers by business.

US WTI crude oil fell below $80 per barrel for the first time since Aug. 10 this week.

CFDs on WTI crude oil one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

For Brooks, tightening policy amid falling oil markets is an “error” that spells acute pain for stocks and the broader risk-asset cohort by driving up real interest rates. “I’ve been banging the drum that markets are heading for full meltdown because the Fed is hiking into falling oil prices, a policy error that’s giving us a super-charged rise in real rates,” he wrote.

On Nov. 28, the second Saturday preceding the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), at which a decision on monetary policy, including the federal funds rate, will be announced, the Fed’s “blackout” period begins. During blackouts, FOMC participants cannot give interviews or otherwise speak in public on monetary policy and macroeconomic developments.

Brooks argues that without efforts to calm markets before the blackout period, selling pressure on risk assets could intensify.

“That’ll bring a full meltdown in markets and we’ll end up not getting a hike on December 9. Unfortunately, this is the path we’re on,” he continued.

The upheaval intensified on Monday, as the US Dollar Index - a measure of the dollar’s strength against a basket of major currencies - hit 104.5, its highest level since March. It has remained above 100 since mid-September.

US Dollar Index one-week chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

At the same time, US stock markets continue to deal with compounding sell-side pressure. On Friday, the S&P 500 fell to 6,882 points, a level last seen in mid-April.

Brooks noted that even Nvidia’s reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang failed to lift investor sentiment. Beyond stocks, meanwhile, gold saw its worst 60-day sell-off in over 40 years.

“It seems increasingly likely that we go into this without a dovish pivot, in which case the wheels might really start coming off in markets,” he concluded.

The latest data from CME FedWatch shows that markets still overwhelmingly expect a 25-basis-point rate hike in December. As of Thursday, the probability of the Fed keeping its target rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% stood at just 0.5%.

Fed target-rate probabilities for Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting. Source: CME Group

#4881. $7 Billion in Bitcoin Options Just Expired: Here’s What It Means

$7 Billion in Bitcoin Options Just Expired: Here’s What It Means

Nearly $6.8 billion worth of Bitcoin options expired Friday on crypto derivatives exchange Deribit, removing roughly a quarter of outstanding Bitcoin options positions from the exchange, according to CryptoQuant.

The expiration comes at a particularly difficult time for Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency traded near $61,000 ahead of settlement before dropping below $59,000 later Friday, extending a brutal November for crypto investors.

Friday’s expiry was considerably smaller than October’s $10.8 billion settlement, but the way traders positioned themselves tells a different story about market sentiment.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Options are financial contracts that give investors the right to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined price, known as the strike price. Call options generally benefit from rising prices, whereas put options can serve as insurance against a decline.

Nearly half of the outstanding $40,000 put positions were scheduled to expire on December 25. That doesn't necessarily mean traders expect Bitcoin to fall that far, but it shows that investors are willing to position themselves against such a scenario.

The estimated “max pain” price for Friday’s expiration stood at $70,000. That's the price at which option holders collectively receive the smallest payout at expiration, around 15% above Bitcoin’s price heading into settlement.

Bitcoin settled at approximately $61,600, leaving many put options with intrinsic value and higher-priced calls worthless.

The expiration does not mean $6.8 billion in Bitcoin changed hands. That figure is just the notional value of the underlying contracts, rather than the amount paid out at expiration.

What could affect Bitcoin's price is the unwinding of positions that market makers accumulated to offset their exposure to those contracts. As those hedges become unnecessary, buying or selling activity associated with them can disappear or reverse, potentially amplifying price movements in either direction.

Bitcoin still faces considerable selling pressure outside the derivatives market.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs registered their seventh consecutive trading session of net withdrawals on Wednesday, bringing November’s total to $5.39 billion.

Accelerating inflation, concerns over U.S. interest rates, and a renewed AI stock selloff have also put pressure on Bitcoin this week.

Traders were paying more for near-term volatility than for volatility further into 2027 ahead of the expiry, which likely means that concerns about Bitcoin’s near-term performance extend well beyond Friday’s settlement.

The next major options expiry is scheduled for Christmas Day, with contracts covering roughly 165,000 BTC, or about $10 billion at Friday’s settlement price.

#4879. Spain moves to grant financial watchdog power to freeze crypto accounts

A new decree would allow Spain’s financial intelligence unit to suspend crypto accounts, with firms facing fines for noncompliance.

A decree published on Nov. 25 would give Spain’s financial intelligence unit, Sepblac, the power to freeze crypto accounts and halt transactions without prior judicial authorization when it suspects money laundering or terrorist financing.

The measures are scheduled to take effect on Jan. 25, 2027. Under Spain’s Constitution, the Congress of Deputies must vote to ratify or repeal the decree within 30 days of its promulgation. If ratified, crypto companies operating in Spain would have to comply with suspension orders or face financial penalties.

According to the decree, Sepblac would be able to suspend the use of a digital asset account or a business relationship for up to five business days, while transactions in progress could be held for up to 10 business days. Although the initial suspension of an account or transaction would be at the discretion of Sepblac, it could be extended by a court at the request of public prosecutors.

Nikolai Timofejev, head of licensing and regulatory affairs at legal consulting firm Prifinance, told Cointelegraph that crypto firms should start preparing for the change before it takes effect. “My advice is to treat it like an operational workstream with a named person who receives Sepblac’s orders,” he said. “Non-compliance amounts to a very serious infringement attracting fines starting at €150,000.”

Timofejev explained that crypto companies should be ready to respond quickly, acting on suspension orders the day they receive them to avoid penalties.

The person in charge of responding to Sepblac’s orders should have the authority to “immediately (same day) freeze client withdrawals and transactions.” Companies affected would be responsible for tracking when each order expires.

Firms are also required to report suspicious activity to Sepblac, which, under the decree, would have three business days to issue a transaction suspension order if warranted.

Timofejev expressed support for the decree, saying he hoped “to see similar measures implemented across the entire EU.”

For crypto service providers operating in Spain, the new rules would add another layer of compliance obligations alongside those established under the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA).

#4878. Samsung Frame Pro TV Review, Tested by AD (2026)

A staple in most modern homes, televisions often war against the ongoing aesthetics of a space in their off-time. Masquerading as artwork, the Samsung Frame TV offers an alternative in the world of home entertainment that amplifies interior design instead of taking away from it.

Eagle eyes will have spotted the Frame across many of our home tours—including some celebrity abodes, like the living room of Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s New York pied-a-terre. With their art-forward ideology, it’s clear to see why the Frame line is favored by designers. After all, a big black screen is not really enhancing the visual impact of a living room.

As a design devotee and AD’s resident television and film-obsessive, I tried out the Frame Pro to see if it really measured up. Boasting the same matte finish display as the original model but with brighter picture quality, fully wireless outputs, and a bevy of technical upgrades, the Frame Pro has features to offer for tech purists and design-heads alike.

How much does it cost? Are there payment plans available?

The Frame Pro starts at $2,200—though is already marked down for Black Friday, and may drop further in price closer to the shopping holiday. Payment plans are available through Affirm, with options up to four installments, the lowest being $400 every two weeks.

The Frame Pro comes in three sizes, starting at 65 inches and going up in ten inch intervals to 85 inches. I opted for the smallest size to best fit my available wall space, and chose a white bezel border (brown and teak are the other colorways) to coordinate with the frames on the wall art in my living room.

A service coordinated the delivery window with me over email and helped to set up the television once they arrived to make sure it was functioning properly. Despite what the name would have you believe, the Frame Pro does, in fact, have attachable legs. The delivery service did not include mounting, so the team merely helped lift the Frame Pro onto my TV stand and set it up in a freestanding format.

What was the installation process like? How long did it take, and how many people?

The Frame Pro has a very slim mounting system consisting of two brackets. The installation kit comes with a paper template with the layout of the brackets printed on it. The process was fairly straightforward, though I wish the step-by-step manual had more text included rather than just showing images of the process.

Although the brackets have several slots to accommodate differing stud widths, we ran into an issue where the distance between the studs in our building didn’t quite align with the bracket slots to center it on the wall while also keeping the TV secure in the studs. In the end, we ended up hanging the TV ever so slightly off-center in order to keep the screws aligned with the studs. For peace of mind, we added drywall anchors and screws to the center-most slots of the bracket for some additional support to help distribute the weight a bit more.

Hanging the TV from the bracket was simple, and because the screw-in panels on the back are magnetized, it made it feel more secure when we slotted it into place. At just under 50 pounds, the TV wasn’t all that heavy, though because of the larger size, we did need two people (and another to guide the way) to lift it in place. The bezel is also magnetized, so the four pieces simply snap onto the exterior of the TV once you have it hung up.

Overall, the mounting process took us about two hours to complete but I think it could likely be decreased down to one hour (and possibly even less) had it not been for our particular issues with the stud distances that needed a lot of remeasuring and even a last-minute trip to the hardware store for a stud finder.

As the Frame’s main draw, I was most eager to see art mode in action. The artwork is selected either through Samsung’s Art Store (which requires a $4.99 per month subscription) or through personally uploaded photos to the SmartThings companion app. To really be convincing as artwork, the photos need to be high quality—you wouldn’t notice any blurriness when seeing the Mona Lisa at the Louvre, would you? For older artworks, I was able to find plenty of high resolution files available for free through museum or crowdsourced websites. Once you make sure its resolution matches the 4K sizing of the Frame (3,840 x 2,160 pixels), you simply upload the image and select if you want a matboard added to the border. If you upload a smaller size image, you can expect to see some amount of graininess once it loads on the screen. I chose a selection of paintings by Vincent Van Gogh, Georgia O’Keefe, and Claude Monet, among other artists with the rotating gallery feature. While essentially all the artwork I tested out looked beautiful on the screen, the paintings with thicker brushstrokes made me want to reach out and touch it to see if it was real.

I found that the art mode is most convincing when you’re in a well-lit room. Even though the TV brightness does adjust automatically—and has motion sensors so it only turns on when someone enters a room if you want to leave it on all day—the fact that it’s a screen becomes more obvious in low-light environments. Even at its lowest brightness setting, when in art mode in a dark room, the screen slightly illuminates the space, no longer tricking your eyes that it’s artwork.

In terms of the viewing experience, the Frame Pro certainly leveled up my weekly binge watches. The image is incredibly crisp, and when rewatching shows I’d seen before (I’m a creature of habit, what can I say), I noticed the colors were markedly more vivid than on my previous TV. The Neo QLED panel, a.k.a. mini LEDs, makes a big difference in the contrast of colors on the TV, and it’s all the more enjoyable to see ingenious set designs from my favorite shows and movies.

One of the big differences between the Frame Pro and previous models is the Wireless One Connect box. Where the regular Frame model has a slim transparent cord connected to the box that contains HDMI and other outputs, the Frame Pro is fully wireless, meaning the only cable coming out of the TV is the power cord. I have fairly speedy and reliable internet so there haven’t been any issues with connection being wireless. Plus, I love the clean look the lack of cords provides. The only time I noticed lag was when I tried using Chromecast from my phone to try and stream content. It took longer to load and had some clarity issues in the picture. That’s not true for everything I cast, as a movie I mirrored through AirPlay loaded easily, so I think it might have been due to an incompatibility with Google’s casting software or the phone it was being routed through.

I’ve had the Frame Pro for over a year now and haven’t noticed any difference in visual quality or functionality when watching different shows or movies. Style-wise, I’ve loved decorating around the Frame as the seasons change. The minimalist white base doesn’t detract from surrounding decor, like pumpkins during Halloween and garland and ornaments around Christmas. I’ve subbed in a few different pieces of artwork in the art library, particularly during hosting season when I want to curate a cozier vibe with an autumnal artwork or yule log video. The automatic software updates keep the TV functioning at a high level, even as streaming apps regularly change.

It’s safe to say that I’m keeping this TV for as long as possible. Even as someone who loves to watch shows and movies, I don’t want the entire design of my living room to revolve around a television. The slim design of the Frame really shifts the focus to the other furniture and decor in the space, and makes my space feel more centered around the memories made inside it.

#4877. Japan weighs tighter oversight of DeFi, self-custodial wallets

Japan’s financial regulator is exploring measures to curb illicit finance risks, including potential restrictions on access to DeFi services.

Japan’s Financial Services Agency (FSA) is weighing potential new regulations for decentralized finance (DeFi) and self-custodial wallet providers as part of a broader effort to address risks associated with onchain finance.

In a discussion paper dated Thursday, the regulator raised the possibility of discouraging users from accessing DeFi services that lack adequate Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing controls.

The FSA also asked whether regulated businesses that interact with DeFi, including stablecoin issuers, on- and off-ramp providers and financial institutions, should play a role in mitigating illicit finance risks when no party responsible for regulatory compliance can be identified.

The regulator questioned how to identify parties responsible for DeFi services that claim to be decentralized but retain centralized elements, and whether front-end providers that give users access to decentralized exchanges should be subject to financial regulation.

The question of who should be held responsible for DeFi activities remains unresolved in other major markets. The European Union excludes fully decentralized crypto services without intermediaries from its Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation, while US regulators have largely focused on the nature of financial activities and the degree of control exercised by developers or operators. The stalled US CLARITY Act seeks to clarify which DeFi participants should be subject to financial regulation.

The FSA noted that direct regulation of self-custodial wallet use and providers that solely develop or sell software or hardware remains uncommon internationally but raised questions about whether additional measures are needed to protect users and prevent illicit financial activity.

Japan already requires domestic virtual asset service providers to collect information and maintain records on transactions involving self-custodial wallets, according to the FSA. Potential anti-fraud measures also include cooling-off periods for transfers from newly opened crypto exchange accounts to self-custodial wallets.

The discussions form part of a broader financial strategy announced by the FSA in July to promote onchain finance, with the initiative’s interim findings targeted for early 2027.

#4876. 4 Scary Bitcoin Charts That Suggest This Bear Market Is Different

4 Scary Bitcoin Charts That Suggest This Bear Market Is Different

Bitcoin fell below $60,000 again on Friday as roughly $6.8 billion worth of Bitcoin options expired on derivatives exchange Deribit earlier in the day.

The largest cryptocurrency by market cap was trading at around $59,576 as of writing, down 1.58% on the daily chart after reaching an intraday high of $62,210.

As you might be able to guess based on the recent price action, Bitcoin's technical setup remains bearish—and there’s four charts in particular that tell the story.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The coin is trading well below its 50-day and 200-day exponential moving averages, or EMAs, which currently sit at $71,112 and $74,444, respectively, with the shorter-term average below the longer-term one—a classically bearish death cross pattern.

Its Relative Strength Index, or RSI, which measures the strength of recent price movements on a scale of 0 to 100, sits at 25.69, putting Bitcoin in oversold territory. Bitcoin is also approaching its 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level at $57,618, a potential support derived from the cryptocurrency's rally between its 2022 bottom and 2025 peak.

A sustained break below that level would put the recent lows back in focus. The next major Fibonacci retracement on the chart sits near $39,000, which would be an absolute nightmare for the markets. Thankfully for Bitcoin holders, BTC has bounced every time it touched it.

Perhaps more concerning for long-term Bitcoin investors, however, is what's happening to some of the most popular models used to make sense of Bitcoin's historical price cycles.

The Bitcoin Power Law model, popularized by physicist Giovanni Santostasi, attempts to explain Bitcoin's price growth as a mathematical function of its age.

Plotting Bitcoin's price and the time elapsed since its creation on logarithmic scales produces a relatively straight trend line. Two parallel lines establish theoretical upper and lower boundaries based on historical price extremes.

The appeal of the model was that Bitcoin's increasingly expensive bear market bottoms appeared remarkably predictable, despite the cryptocurrency's notorious volatility.

Bitcoin is now trading below what crypto analytics provider Bitbo sets as the theoretical support line of approximately $68,600, while the model's central regression puts its price near $193,400.

That's roughly 69% below its theoretical valuation, and 13% below what was supposed to be its historical floor.

The breach challenges one of the model's most attractive assumptions: that Bitcoin's minimum price increases predictably over time.

Bitcoin's four-year market cycle revolves around the halving, a programmed event that cuts the issuance of new Bitcoin tokens by 50% approximately every four years.

The most recent halving, in April 2024, reduced the reward miners receive for producing a block from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC.

Bitbo's post-halving comparison chart takes the price performance following the 2012, 2016 and 2020 halvings and adjusts those returns to Bitcoin's price at the start of the 2024 cycle.

Had Bitcoin replicated its performance following the 2020 halving, it would currently be trading somewhere around $140,000. Matching the returns of its earlier cycles would imply prices of several hundred thousand dollars or more.

Instead, roughly 950 days after its most recent halving, Bitcoin is trading below where it was when that cycle began.

Diminishing returns are nothing new for Bitcoin as the asset grows larger. But the scale of the current underperformance raises questions about how useful previous halving cycles remain as a guide to future returns.

It also shows traders are a bit less enthusiastic about the upcoming halving vs previous times—maybe because Bitcoin is now more mainstream and the user base is more diverse and less interested in those technicalities.

The Bitcoin Rainbow Chart, which originated in 2014, uses logarithmic price curves and colored bands to classify Bitcoin's historical valuation.

The upper red bands represent speculative bubbles, while the lower blue and violet bands indicate historically depressed prices.

Bitcoin's price has dropped beneath even the violet region, humorously labeled “Bitcoin Dead,” in the supplied chart.

This isn't the first time the Rainbow Chart has struggled to accommodate Bitcoin's price movements. Its creator revised the model in November 2022 after the previous version failed to contain that year's market collapse.

The chart is ultimately a visualization of historical price behavior rather than a scientifically validated valuation model. Its latest divergence is another reminder of that limitation.

Bitbo's price prediction comparison brings together four different approaches to estimating Bitcoin's long-term value.

The Stock-to-Flow model, introduced by pseudonymous analyst PlanB in 2019, measures scarcity by comparing Bitcoin's existing supply with its annual issuance. Stock-to-Income expands on that concept by incorporating miners' transaction fee revenue and regularly updating its calculations.

The Power Law measures price growth over time, while the Halving Price Regression fits a curve using historical prices at halving dates, excluding much of the speculative activity between them.

In the chart's late-2026 projections, Stock-to-Flow puts Bitcoin near $397,535, followed by the Power Law at $198,495, Stock-to-Income at $173,412, and Halving Price Regression at $141,132.

Bitcoin is trading approximately 85% below the most optimistic of those projections and 58% below even the most conservative one.

None of these models directly measures how much money investors are willing to put into Bitcoin today, and arguably Bitcoin is now a different asset than the BTC we used to follow two years ago.

It’s possible that after the wave of ETFs, funds, derivatives, 401Ks, regulations, indicators tracking its price, and widespread access to retail investors, it’s these price-prediction models that need to change.

#4875. 16 Best Strength Training Exercises to Build Muscle and Strength Fast

There’s no shortage of strength training exercises to pepper into your muscle-building routine. If you’re a regular on FitTok, you might’ve noticed that a new exercise seems to pop up regularly. So, which ones should you pepper into your routine?

“It all comes down to your goal,” says Angela Gargano, a trainer and creator of Strong Feels Good & Pull-up Revolution. The exercises you fill your program with are your most important tools for success.

Keep reading for the best strength training exercises to try, exactly how to add them into a total-body routine, and expert-backed tips for making a plan that works. Ready to get lifting?

Build lasting strength with the WH+ Strong Over 50 Plan, here

Below, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite strength training exercises, spanning all the different muscle groups. Here’s how to create a well-rounded full-body routine you can do regularly.

Equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebell, resistance band | Good for: Total body Instructions: Pick one move from each category—push, pull, hinge, lunge, squat—to create a total body workout. Do it two to three days a week, preferably on nonconsecutive days. For each move, do the allocated amount of sets and reps, resting for 1 to 2 minutes between sets. Select weights that make the last few reps challenging, but doable (and more on selecting weights, below!).

Alternatively, you can split up muscle groups if you have multiple days a week to work out (if you’re working out only two days a week or less, stick with a full-body plan). There are a few ways to do this. If you're planning on strength training twice a week, you can also opt to do one upper-body day (the push/pull exercises) and one lower-body day (the hinge/lunge/squat exercises). Select four or five exercises with a variety of exercise type (don’t fill a lower body day with only squats, no matter how much you love them!) to create your workout.

Or, if you're working out three times a week, you can split your workouts to do one push/pull day, and two hinge/lunge/squat days, or vice versa, depending on what part of your body you want to strengthen most. If you're training more than three times a week, you can split by muscle group.

Here are 16 of the best strength training exercises to fill in your workout.

Why it rocks: Pushups are a classic move for a reason: They work your chest, shoulders, and triceps. Another perk? They engage your core muscles and build functional strength.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 or 4 sets of 8 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Unlike a standard shoulder press, this upper-body exercise challenges all three muscle heads of your deltoids.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Triceps extensions are killer for isolating and strengthening your triceps muscles for improved strength and functionality.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: You’ll strengthen your lats, traps, and delts with this classic upper-body pull move. The bent-over position provides a little extra challenge to your core, too.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps.

Why it rocks: This is an excellent bent-over row variation that targets your lats and rhomboids, requiring less core stability than a traditional bent-over row.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: You’ll strengthen your lats, traps, and delts with this upper-body movement. “This exercise is so beneficial because you are working in a hinged position and teaching your body how to properly brace,” Harvey notes. “This will come in handy the next time you need to bend over and pick something up.”

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Deadlifts build overall strength and power in the posterior chain muscles, including the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps.

Why it rocks: This move strengthens your lower body while also improving stability, and the resistance band is great for added intensity.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps each side.

Why it rocks: This beginner-friendly move works your glutes, core, and lower back, and may help mitigate back discomfort due to sitting.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 8 to 10 reps.

Why it rocks: Reverse lunges work the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes, all while improving coordination and stability.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps each side.

Why it rocks: Curtsy lunges torch the glutes and outer thighs, while also improving lower body strength and muscle symmetry.

Why it rocks: In addition to working your outer glute muscles and upper legs, this move helps promote stability and balance in your lower body.

Why it rocks: Holding an object like a kettlebell (though you can also use a dumbbell) at chest height calls your core more in on the action—training your body proper core activation that will allow you to push heavier as you get stronger.

Why it rocks: The Bulgarian split squat can shore up functional strength unilaterally, helping to correct any imbalances.

Why it rocks: This move improves single-leg balance by promoting unilateral strength. Plus, it's easily adaptable since you can change the height of the step and the weight you're holding.

Why it rocks: With a wider stance than used in a traditional squat, this move builds quad and glute strength, and also increases hip mobility.

Strength training can help you build and maintain muscle mass, improve your joint and bone health, support better body composition, and even increase your longevity. And, including it in your routine is easy to do, as long as you follow these tips and tricks.

“The biggest thing in putting together your entire workout is making sure that you have a proper warm-up, always, no matter what,” says Gargano. “People tend to throw that out the window but dynamic moves are going to help you wake the body up a little bit before you get into your strength training.”

To execute a proper warm-up, select 3 to 4 dynamic and mobility exercises (these are a few of our favorites!) and do them for 30 seconds apiece, 2 or 3 times through. If you're planning on exercising a specific part of your body that day, make sure your warm-up is tailored to that (e.g., if you're about to do a leg day lift, select a few warm-up moves that promote blood flow to the lower body, like lateral lunges or the World's Greatest Stretch).

“In your programming, there’s a combination of things you should always have,” says Gargano, noting you don’t have to put them all in the same workout/day, but they should certainly all fit in your week: Push movements (like pushups and chest presses), pull movements (like pull-ups and rows), squats, lunges, and hinge movements (think: deadlifts, hip hinges).

Programming your workouts will largely depend on how many times a week you work out (more on that here). The more times a week you can exercise, the more you can split your workouts by muscle group. For example, if you're working out three days per week, you might be interested in doing one upper-body day, one leg day focused on glutes and hamstrings, and another focused on quads and calves. If you're only working out twice per week, you'll want to make sure you're programming for the whole body: at least one upper-body lift and one lower-body lift.

“I know people are going to be like, ‘Well, what about my core?’ but your core is used in all those movements,” Gargano assures.

“You want to be sure that you're working all the body parts so that you're not uneven,” says Gargano. It's an issue trainers see a lot—people focus so hard on defining one part of their body that they neglect the rest. For example, if you're aiming to build up your glutes, don't only do hip thrusts on lower body day. Incorporate some lunges and squats in there, too, to strengthen your quad muscles so they can work in tandem with your strong glutes.

As long as you hit all five of the main movement patterns we named earlier (push, pull, squat, lunge, hip hinge) throughout the week, you should be in good shape.

A few weeks into your workout program, your body will get used to what you’re doing—so you'll need to level up the challenge, “so that your body can continue to develop and work the muscles in different ways,” says Gargano. That means increasing your weights, reps, or sets to progressively overload the muscles—doing so will help them get continuously stronger, and ensure your performance never plateaus.

To know when to up the weights, use the two-for-two rule: Once you can do two extra good-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load. From there, try to increase 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. But remember, this is just a recommendation—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

The best exercise plan is the one you're going to stick to. And the one you're going to stick to is the one that best fits into your schedule.

“You need to figure out what is working well for you and your body,” says Gargano. “Everybody's different, so try out two days a week first, and then if you feel good, maybe add that third day.”

Once you have your schedule set, don't feel like it's an end-all, be-all. The more you can hit your workouts, the better—but there's no reason to knock yourself down if things get busy and you miss one or two. You can always abbreviate your workout by cutting a few exercises or sets, or get moving by going for a brief walk. The key is to stay moving as much as you can. It won't always be perfect, and that's okay.

#4874. UK is ‘getting it wrong’ on DeFi regulation, says Coinbase

Coinbase and Stand With Crypto argue that the FCA’s proposed DeFi rules could leave UK users without regulated access to decentralized finance.

Coinbase and Stand With Crypto, a crypto advocacy group backed by the exchange, are pushing back against the UK’s proposed approach to decentralized finance (DeFi), arguing that restrictions on regulated crypto platforms could leave consumers with fewer safeguards when accessing DeFi services.

The criticism follows reports on Nov. 26 that the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) plans to proceed with tighter rules and authorization requirements for DeFi platforms, citing money laundering risks exposed by the $6.3 billion Binance hack. Although the attack targeted a centralized exchange, hackers moved stolen funds through decentralized protocols, complicating efforts to trace and freeze the assets.

Katie Harries, head of policy for Europe at Coinbase, said the proposals could limit opportunities for regulated firms to work with authorities on consumer safeguards.

“The UK is getting its approach to DeFi wrong,” Harries told Cointelegraph. “This isn’t a ban on UK consumers using DeFi; it’s a ban on giving them a regulated route to use it.”

In an October opinion piece for Cointelegraph, Harries argued that the proposed framework could effectively prevent regulated crypto platforms from offering DeFi services, as requirements to execute customer orders through authorized trading venues could exclude decentralized protocols with no central operator capable of obtaining FCA authorization.

Related: Japan weighs tighter oversight of DeFi, self-custodial wallets

Harries argued that regulated platforms could help address the FCA’s concerns around DeFi through due diligence and safeguards.

The FCA has previously used regulatory sandboxes to allow financial services firms to test new products in live markets under regulatory oversight. On Feb. 25, the regulator named four regulated entities to test out stablecoin products within its regulatory sandbox.

“The UK has got a lot right on crypto, but its approach is closing the door on DeFi innovation,” Harries said.

Harry Pearce-Gould, general manager at Stand With Crypto, argued that the proposals could leave UK users with fewer options for accessing DeFi services. “That leaves UK crypto users without the trusted, regulated routes to access DeFi that will be available to people doing the same thing in other jurisdictions.”

He said people should be able to use crypto for financial activities such as borrowing against their holdings, provided they have clear information about the associated risks.

The implications could extend beyond consumer protection, potentially putting the UK at a competitive disadvantage in the digital asset industry, according to Harries. “The UK is creating a prohibition, and that doesn’t sit right with its ambition to be a global centre for digital assets,” she said.

The FCA closed consultations on its proposed DeFi guidance and wider crypto regulatory framework on Nov. 18, with final guidance expected in January 2027. The new regime is scheduled to take effect on Oct. 25, 2027.

Related: Binance says it obtained $6.5B worldwide freezing order after hack

All to say: if you're going to invest in a rug, you might as well get a good deal. Now is that time.

In the current bargain bin, you’ll find rugs spanning the shape, color, and pattern spectrum.

#4872. Lifting Heavy Isn’t the Whole Story When It Comes to Building Strength. Here's What to Do Instead.

My name is Cori Ritchey, and I am an exercise physiology nerd turned fitness journalist, and the fitness editor at Women’s Health. When I’m not writing, editing, and researching fitness, I’m teaching it to my personal training and group fitness clients. In my new column, Between Sets, I’m pulling back the curtain on the same advice, tips, and ‘aha!’ moments I share with my clients while they’re catching their breath. Stick around for the strategic, science-backed nuggets that’ll help you move better, train smarter, and actually enjoy the process.

Scroll any fitness feed and you’ll see it: people clanging plates, chasing PRs, and even pulling dangerous stunts for the pride of lifting heavy. And where there’s real joy in getting stronger, there’s also real pressure to keep adding weight.

As a strength and conditioning coach and the fitness editor at Women’s Health, I’ve been preaching the lift-heavy-or-go-home gospel for years. For valid reason: challenging your muscles over time is one of the most reliable ways to build lasting strength, support bone health, improve body composition, and stay functional as we age.

The “lift heavy” ethos isn’t new. Strength training is as old as Ancient Greece, where the first gyms were developed. It progressed through decades of physical culture into Muscle Beach, USA, the birthplace of American lifting that started as a beachside gymnastics park in Venice Beach, California, in the 1940s. It was there, too, where the first American women bodybuilders, like legendary Abbey Stockton, emerged—at a time when many scientists still believed lifting was bad for the body.

Research eventually caught up to what lifters were already experiencing: resistance training works. More women, especially in recent years, started showing up for it, too. In 2004, 17 percent of women reported regularly participating in weight lifting. By 2020, that number has bumped to nearly 30 percent. Then came the influencer era, amplifying a message that’s equal parts motivating and misleading: lifting weights is good for you—but it has to be heavy to count.

There’s a kernel of truth in there. Progressive overload (the process of gradually increasing the stress you put on your body in a workout) builds muscle and strength, and increasing load is an efficient way to do so.

And that matters—especially when heavier, heavier, heavier simply isn’t in the cards.

Because for many, it’s not. It requires access to specific equipment, time to train consistently without rushing through sets, and quality coaching and information to nail form and stay injury-free. It also has to be safe and appropriate for your body on any given day—whether you’re navigating chronic illness, postpartum or perimenopause realities, and injury history, or limiting pain. And even when everything lines up on paper, there’s a very real mental hurdle: walking into a gym and loading up a bar can be intimidating as hell.

Still, if you’re here to build strength, change your body composition, protect your bone health, or invest in your movement longevity, lifting heavier will certainly help—but it’s not the only path to lifelong strength. Somewhere along the way, “heavy” became synonymous with “effective”, and “light” or "moderate" became codes for “waste of time.”

The exercise research world is finding that’s not the case. “You don't need to do anything heavy for the health benefits of resistance exercise to take place,” says Stuart Phillips, PhD, kinesiology professor and hypertrophy researcher at McMaster University.

Adequate research has suggested that hypertrophy (the fancy scientific term for muscle growth) is not determined by a magic rep goal or the weight on the bar, says Susie Reiner, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, assistant professor of exercise science at Seton Hall University, and CEO of TheoryEx, a sport science research and consulting firm. “Instead, hypertrophy appears to be driven by whether a training set provides a sufficiently strong internal stimulus to the muscle, which is reasonably defined as effort and proximity to muscular failure.”

Trainers have traditionally been taught that specific rep ranges map neatly to specific goals: 1 to 3 for power, 3 to 8 for strength, 8 to 12 for muscle, and 12-plus for muscular endurance. But newer findings show you can build muscle across a much wider rep range—roughly as low as 5 and as high as 25, Phillips says. “There is, then, by definition, no sweet spot for muscle building, because the whole repetition range then becomes the sweet spot.”

Across several studies and meta-analyses, similar muscle growth has been seen between people who train with lighter loads (about 30 to 40 percent of their one-rep maximum), and those who train with heavier loads (about 70 to 85 percent of their one-rep maximum)—as long as sets are taken close enough to failure.

Muscle growth is dependent on recruiting and fatiguing a large portion of muscle fibers, Reiner says. Your muscles need a reason to adapt. With heavier weights for fewer reps, you recruit a lot of fibers immediately. With lighter weights for higher reps, you recruit them more gradually.

One thing to note here: while a large percentage of these studies have only been done in men, Phillips notes that “the work that has been done in women shows us that actually men and women respond very, very similarly to weight lifting in terms of muscle mass gain. Women have less baseline muscle, but relatively speaking, they gain the same amount as men—that's been robustly shown.” Phillips and his colleagues are currently running several studies (including one study specific to perimenopausal women!) that will further clarify what this looks like in women.

Researchers feel confident that as long as sets are taken sufficiently to failure (more on what that means coming up), different loading strategies can produce similar hypertrophy, Reiner says.

Here’s what that looks like IRL: Let’s say you have biceps curls on your workout plan each week. One week, you pick up the 10-pound dumbbells, and do 3 sets of 12 reps. In the sets, when you approach the end of that rep range, it feels tough—you can maybe grind out 2 more reps max. The next week, you reach for the 15s. You can only hit 6 reps before you feel like your form is faltering, but the effort feels similar—you’ve still got about two reps left before your form breaks down.

The heavier weight might feel more empowering, but both workouts deliver a similar muscle-building stimulus—assuming you’re training regularly enough, eating enough protein and calories, and adequately recovering, of course.

Sure, research confirms you don’t have to lift crazy heavy—but that doesn’t mean that coming close to failure feels easy. Failing a rep can be scary (and honestly, discouraging). Here’s the good news: you don’t need true, all-out failure. You just need to train to proximity to failure.

One practical way to gauge that is with the rate of perceived exertion scale. “Rate of perceived exertion (RPE) is a global effort scale, typically ranging from one to 10,” Reiner says. An RPE of 10 represents maximal effort—no chance you could do one more rep. A RPE of nine suggests you could do one more, an RPE of eight means you could probably do two more reps, and so on and so forth.

Muscle growth still occurs between RPE of 7 to 9, Phillips says. “You don’t need it to be a 10 out of 10 where you’re red-lining and can’t get the bar off your chest.” In other words: you can train hard without routinely hitting the point where things get sketchy.

That matters, because the closer you get to all-out failure, the more your injury risk can creep up—especially if you start twisting, bouncing, and compensating to force a rep you simply don’t have.

The failure you want to flirt with is technical failure, or technical fatigue. “Technical failure means you cannot complete another repetition with good form,” Phillips says—that’s where injury risk rises. Muscular failure (otherwise known as momentary failure) occurs when a muscle is unable to generate enough force to complete another rep, regardless of maximal effort. Picture trying to do one more biceps curl and you quite literally cannot lift your arm and the weight up again—that’s muscular failure..

Aim for technical failure. Pushing yourself too far in an effort to achieve muscular failure could cause your body to overcompensate and push you into a compromising position. The good news, too, is technical failure tends to be very close to muscular failure for most people, Phillips says.

A useful rule of thumb: stop when you have one to two perfect-form reps left in the tank.

Yes, you still need to reach for that RPE of 7 to 9—but there’s more ways to do that than just reaching for the next highest weight. Here are some other elements you can play with to up the challenge:

Frequency. Reaching for heavier weights, you can simply aim to reach for any type of weight more often. That might look like increasing your strength training days from two to three days a week.

Volume. Think of your training volume as the amount of weight total you lift during a given session. Sure, lifting heavier loads is one way to increase your total, but it can also be accomplished by increasing the amount of sets or reps you do.

Rest time. Decreasing the amount of rest you allow yourself gives your muscles less time to recover, wearing them out quicker with lighter loads.

Time under tension. The amount of time your muscles work for matters. Increasing your time under tension, or the amount of time your muscles are working in a lift (for example, lowering a curl for a slow four-count).

That all being said, heavier loads might still take the cake in terms of efficiency. You’ll find yourself increasing your frequency and volume to monotonous levels if you never increase your load.

Back to biceps curls: Say you get comfortable at six reps at 15 lbs. After a few weeks, it no longer starts to feel challenging for you, so you increase it eight. And then 10. And then 12. If you never reach for the intimidating 20 lb dumbbells, you’ll eventually find yourself having to do sets of 30 reps just to feel something. And that can become time consuming. You don’t need extremes all the time—but you do need your training to stay challenging.

“For individuals who are uncomfortable training to very high levels of effort, consistent training at moderate-to-high RPEs combined with sufficient volume and progression can still produce meaningful muscle growth,” Reiner says. “From a long-term perspective, hypertrophy depends less on any single maximal set and more on repeated exposure to challenging, well-managed training over weeks and months.”

Convinced to start pushing closer to failure? Here are a few ways to progress safely.

The two-for-two method is a classic progression strategy used by professional trainers. Once you can do two extra proper-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load.

Let's use the biceps curl example just one more time. You’ve been training with the 15s for sets of 8, and now you can hit 10 with clean form for two workouts in a row. That’s your cue to grab 17.5s the next go.

How much should you increase, exactly? The National Strength and Conditioning Association’s guideline is 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. Reminder that this is just a general guide—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

Trying heavier weights is way less intimidating when you have a safety net.

If you’re nervous, ask for a spot. Maybe you already have a gym buddy you workout with regularly that can help pull the barbell up if you get stuck on a bench press. If you don’t, ask one of your gym’s trainers or employees. Most people will politely oblige, and will even appreciate your effort in challenging yourself.

Have a conversation with your spotter before you get into the lift. Tell them how many reps you’re aiming for, and a cue you’ll give them when you want them to jump in and help (my go-to is a simple “now”—since that’s about all you can get out when you’re out of breath).

Some days just don’t feel as strong as others. Maybe you didn’t sleep super well last night, stressed about work, or are at a tough point in your cycle. That’s life. When that happens, you need to respect the cues your body gives you.

If your warmup sets feel unusually heavy, take the hint: this just might not be the day to pick up that heavy weight. It doesn’t mean you’ve regressing, it’s just a bump in the road. Strength, and muscle building, is not a linear process.

Build muscle with the WH+ Build & Burn series

Ultimately, building and maintaining muscle mass is one of the strongest investments you can make in long-term health—especially as you age.

And lifting heavy is one effective way to provide muscle-building stimulus to the body—but it isn’t accessible, comfortable, or safe for everyone all the time. The goal is progressive challenge, and lighter loads can deliver that when you train with intention and effort.

“You do not need to lift heavy to build muscle, but you do need to train with intention,” Reiner says. “The best approach is the one that someone can perform consistently, safely, and with enough effort to challenge the muscle over time.”

Cori Ritchey, C.S.C.S., is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and condition coach and group fitness instructor. She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

#4870. Could AI Break Bitcoin? Not Yet, Research Firm K33 Says

Could AI Break Bitcoin? Not Yet, Research Firm K33 Says

Recent AI-assisted advances in mathematics have reignited worries about the cryptography underpinning Bitcoin, but there’s no evidence the network’s security has actually been broken, according to a report from research and brokerage firm K33.

The analysts, writing Friday, said AI’s rapid progress in math warrants closer attention to Bitcoin’s defenses, while cautioning against mistaking theoretical breakthroughs for a practical attack.

“Naturally, this has reignited fears surrounding the mathematical assumptions underpinning Bitcoin and modern cryptography,” they wrote, adding that the developments do not themselves offer a way to crack those systems.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The spark was a draft proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of math’s most famous open problems, published last week by Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge with help from the company’s Claude model.

As Decrypt reported, the proof passed independent computational verification, though academic review is ongoing. Its arrival stoked speculation about whether AI could eventually unravel the math securing digital assets.

K33 pushed back on the alarm. Bitcoin’s transaction signatures rely on elliptic curve cryptography, which hinges on how hard it is to derive a private key from a public one, even though the reverse is easy.

The firm noted that the Riemann proof provides no method for attacking that, and that the deeper “P versus NP” question at the heart of such fears remains unsolved. Even if someone proved P equals NP, K33 said, that wouldn’t necessarily yield a usable algorithm, or one that could run fast enough to recover a private key in any practical timeframe.

Conversely, proving P does not equal NP wouldn’t guarantee Bitcoin’s safety either, since faster attack algorithms could still emerge.

The report lands as the broader industry takes the AI-cryptography threat increasingly seriously. The Ethereum Foundation recently flagged AI as a more urgent danger than quantum computing, given its ability to find software flaws and sharpen existing algorithms.

K33 noted the Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and recommended the Keccak-256 hash function for a post-quantum transition it aims to complete by 2029.

The takeaway, per K33, is vigilance without panic.

AI’s mathematical leaps deserve monitoring, and crypto networks are right to harden their cryptography against future threats, but as things stand, Bitcoin’s defenses remain as sound as they were at launch, with no demonstrated compromise.

#4869. The Secrets to Whole-Life Training

A well-rounded fitness routine that will enhance all of your activities and adventures starts with your feet.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There’s more to getting fit than chasing a PR or sweating through another bootcamp class. The real payoff? Being ready for the next workout, the weekend adventure, the everyday hustle, and all the years ahead.

The key is making different types of exercise work together, rather than relying on any one activity. This multifaceted and well-rounded approach to training means you’re working more than the muscles, because you’re focused on the movements.

When you approach training this way, you’re literally starting from the ground up. “Every single step you take, your foot is the first thing that hits the ground,” says Jen Perez, DC, a chiropractic physician who combines clinical practice and education to help people improve foot health and lower-body function. “It’s the first thing that interfaces with the world around you, what has to be strong and springy when you want to run or jump or dance or ski.”

A whole-life, well-rounded training plan comes down to five essentials, according to Courtney Conley, DC, a best-selling author and chiropractic physician with more than two decades of clinical experience:

Cardio and strength may already be part of your routine, but the others can be easier to overlook; especially because they deliver numerous movement benefits that you may not equate them with. For example, Conley emphasizes that power training isn’t just for athletes; it also has practical life applications. “Getting up and out of your chair, having good reaction time, and making sure you don’t fall if you step off a curb and trip are all part of that category,” she says.

Mobility means moving freely through a full range of motion, while balance helps you adjust to changing surfaces and react when your footing shifts—it isn’t just holding a tree pose. “There are thousands of nerve endings in each foot that help communicate to our brain where we are in space,” Perez explains. That feedback, combined with the feet’s ability to grip the ground, helps keep you steady.

Recovery is what allows your body to benefit from hard training, yet Conley says it’s often ignored: “I think one of the biggest mistakes is that people don’t recover.” Sleep, adequate nutrition, and lighter days that deliberately scale back workout volume or intensity give your body time to adapt and help you come back ready for your next workout.

The work you do in the gym should go beyond just trying to look good and prepare you for the demands of everyday movement. For strength and power work, Conley recommends deadlifts and kettlebell swings to train the hip-hinge pattern, along with farmer’s carries to build strength in the core and lower body. “I love all that functional movement,” she says. “A sled push is also great, because as your heel comes off the ground, you’re hitting all the intrinsic muscles of your foot.”

Certain machine exercises may not seem so functional but can address specific weaknesses. For instance, Conley says she often uses seated calf raises to strengthen the tissues around the Achilles and leg extensions to isolate the quadriceps. She also recommends plyometrics—quick, explosive jumping and hopping drills—to develop power. “Try double-leg and single-leg hops, forward and backward, side to side, and zigzag moves,” she says, recommending five or six sets of 10 reps per exercise for plyometric movements.

Ankle and big-toe mobility are number one on Conley’s priority list for things you should focus on outside of your regular workouts. “When you can’t propel through the ankle, you’re going to get there by extending the knee so you can push yourself forward,” she says. “People come in with knee or back pain when oftentimes it’s an ankle problem.” She suggests making mobility a regular part of the week rather than waiting until something feels stiff or restricted. Even a short dedicated session can help you maintain the range of motion your training requires.

Perez says your feet also adapt to the surface beneath you and absorb force. “If you think of your foot like a trampoline, every single step we take, whether walking or running, the foot needs to be able to lower, which is that mobility piece, then it needs to be able to spring back up.”

Perez recommends two simple drills to improve foot mobility and strength: the Foot Handshake, where you weave the fingers of one hand between the toes of the opposite foot and gently circle the foot at the ankle; and Lift, Spread, and Reach, where you lift all five toes, spread them apart, then reach them forward as you lower them.

Another way you can activate your feet during training is to choose your shoes wisely. When it comes to footwear, Perez has one non-negotiable regardless of the activity: a wide toe box that lets your toes spread naturally. “If your toes are more narrow than the ball of your foot, that tells me we’ve got some work to do,” she says. In practice, that can mean adding foot mobility and strength drills to your routine and choosing shoes that let your toes spread naturally.

Perez favors Altra Fit, both for her own footwear and when recommending shoes to others, because it gives the forefoot more room than a traditionally tapered toe box. Conley’s experience shows how the amount of cushioning that feels right can change over time as your foot gets stronger and needs more targeted footwear. She started out in the Altra FWD VIA 2, a cushioned shoe with the original (read: roomiest) FootShape™ and a 4 mm drop that felt familiar coming from conventional running shoes. “I was getting some toe splay and my foot was getting stronger,” she recalls. “Now I put them on, and it’s too much shoe for me because I don’t need as much cushioning.”

That’s where having options comes in. Altra’s Torin 9 offers a more moderate level of cushioning, standard footshape (secure midfoot), and a zero-drop platform that is good for running and still takes advantage of the Altra Fit that helps your feet get stronger as you log miles. For a lower-profile option, the Altra Escalante 5 has low cushioning, a 24 mm stack height, zero drop, and the original, roomiest FootShape fit.

“You’ll want to use the least amount of shoe assistance necessary for the activity,” Perez recommends. A lower-profile, more flexible shoe, like the Escalante 5, offers more ground feel for strength training, while extra cushioning or rocker geometry, found in the Torin 9 and FWD VIA 2, may be useful on longer runs. Conley agrees that a plush running shoe isn’t necessarily the best tool for lifting. “You can’t feel the ground,” she says of maximalist shoes. “You’re standing on something that decreases your sensory acuity.”

If multidimensional fitness is new to you, Conley recommends starting with manageable strength work (two or three days a week), walking, and one or two mobility or foot exercises, and build gradually as your strength and capacity improve. “Do things that challenge you, but not to the point where you start to feel overwhelmed,” she says.

If you already work out or run regularly, consider what’s missing from your routine while prioritizing your main goal. Conley suggests making room for mobility, balance, and power work, and fitting short foot-strength and mobility exercises into existing workouts. Do it while you’re fresh, adjusting your workload when running volume increases or recovery suffers.

The goal isn’t to do everything all the time or become an expert at every type of training. It’s to build a body that can keep doing the things you love. Run the trails. Lift the heavy stuff. Hike the mountain. Get down on the floor with your kids and grandkids—and have the strength and mobility to get back up again.

#4868. BNB Chain details new layer-1 for trading, private finance and AI

The proposed network will operate alongside BNB Smart Chain and retain BNB as its native token, with a public testnet targeted for the first quarter of 2027.

BNB Chain has outlined plans for a new layer-1 blockchain designed to support high-frequency trading, payments, private financial transactions and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

According to a litepaper published Thursday, the network would operate alongside the existing BNB Smart Chain (BSC) and use BNB as its native token, with no new native token planned. The blockchain is currently running as a development network, with BNB Chain targeting a public testnet launch in the first quarter of 2027 and a mainnet launch in the second half of the year.

On general-purpose blockchains, applications typically compete for block space. The proposed network would reserve a portion of its transaction capacity for specific activities, such as payments services, which BNB Chain said could reduce competition for network resources during periods of high demand.

The proposed network would also feature an optional shielded pool designed to support private transfers involving BNB and other supported tokens, including certain decentralized finance (DeFi) transactions. Some transaction details would remain publicly visible, and BNB Chain’s documentation warns that the pool’s circuits remain unaudited and that it should not be used with real funds.

Other proposed features would allow users to transact without first acquiring BNB to pay network fees and authorize AI agents to execute transactions within predefined limits.

OpenAI Turns the Tables on Apple With Its Own Trade-Secret Theft Claims

OpenAI has turned the tables on Apple, filing a countersuit that accuses the iPhone maker of stealing its trade secrets and pressuring hardware suppliers to freeze the ChatGPT maker out, escalating a legal brawl over the race to build the next must-have AI gadget.

The counterclaims, filed Friday in federal court in San Jose, California, flip the script on a dispute Apple started in July, when it sued OpenAI, its io Products hardware unit and two former Apple employees, Tang Tan and Chang Liu, accusing them of carrying confidential hardware secrets to OpenAI to help build a competing device.

OpenAI denied those claims and cast Apple’s suit as an attempt to choke off its ability to hire Apple talent.

Now OpenAI is alleging misconduct of Apple’s own. In the filing, the company accuses Apple of “coercing and threatening” suppliers that work with both firms, including asking shared manufacturers to identify which personnel were assigned to OpenAI projects and pressuring at least one vendor to stop work.

OpenAI also claims a former OpenAI employee who returned to Apple took details about its product plans and suppliers with them, an inversion of Apple’s original accusation.

The countersuit brings claims including federal trade-secret theft, interference with contracts and unfair competition under California law. OpenAI argues Apple sued because it is losing the AI race, asserting in the complaint that the company “has struggled to incorporate innovative AI capabilities into its previously popular products” and is trying to “compete unfairly by any means available.”

It also contends Apple’s employment and exit policies create “trapdoors” designed to let it accuse departing staff of theft.

The reciprocal accusations underscore how high the stakes have climbed in the contest to define the hardware of the AI era. The earlier phase of the case grew contentious over discovery, with OpenAI’s internal emails and text messages drawn into the fight.

A judge indicated the court was “highly likely” to grant Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction, and in October OpenAI pledged not to use the Apple trade secrets at the center of the suit.

Apple has previously said its investigation turned up no OpenAI confidential information. Its original lawsuit is set for trial on July 19, 2027.
