#4806. 8 Best Modular Sofas, Tested And Reviewed by AD's Editors 2026

At one time, a modular sofa looked like it could have been toy furniture—each section clearly delineated. Now, seamless design allows this category of sectionals to look like traditional couches that happen to come apart in easy-to-move pieces. Better yet, this style allows you to customize furniture as your space changes. Whether you’re moving from a small apartment into a spacious four-bedroom and need to grow your seating, or you want to downsize a hulking U-shaped basement sectional into a love seat for a bedroom nook, a modular sectional is the way to go.

Style options abound for sectionals, from the artsy armless Sarah Sherman Samuel design for Lulu and Georgia to the minimalist Castlery and the iconic “Chiclet” silhouette made with injection-molded cushions from Herman Miller.

Moving around the sofa pieces is a cinch with user-friendly connector mechanisms, like slide-in glides and easy-to-configure brackets. It took contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert less than 30 minutes to maneuver the pieces of both her Burrow and Cozey modular sectionals into place. Better yet, most of the best modular sofas on this list come with white-glove delivery, so all you have to do is open the door when it arrives.

You can go as big or as small as you’d like with the Jonathan Chaise Sectional from Castlery, a modular option that starts as a two-seater and builds out to accommodate up to six. “This sofa is incredibly comfortable and feels very well-made,” contributor Rachel Fletcher says in her review. “I’d actually say it’s closer to my mattress in terms of firmness—medium firm to firm—which I very much appreciate. It’s not the kind of sofa you’re going to sink into, quicksand-style, and there’s absolutely no sagging effect.

The minimal, low-slung sofa works great in an understated space and could also appeal to a household with kids and pets. “Castlery does offer swatches and fabric samples, but I went all in without testing first and wasn’t sure what a polyester blend might feel like,” she adds. “Thankfully, it’s very soft. It’s made to resemble wool, but without the itchiness or stiffness. The heathered fabric makes it look expensive and should also help hide stains.”

The Cozey Neptune is a modular sofa that’s a jack of all trades: It can be assembled in less than half an hour, pulls out into a sleeper in two minutes flat, has hidden storage under the cushions, and is available in performance fabrics that protect against spills. Alpert chose the sofa for all those reasons, but what ultimately made the Neptune such a keeper for her was its portability. “I had no problem bringing it into the basement,” she says in her review, despite some tight angles on the landing. “Anyone who lives in a walk-up, has a tight stairway, or has narrow doorways typical of older homes will love this piece.”

Once fully assembled, it proved to be as durable as it is good-looking, treading the line between minimalism and groundedness. “I am very skeptical of couches with cushions on the back because I know that these can collapse, and that will drive me crazy,” Alpert explains. “This back is tightly upholstered, but it comes with three lumbar cushions that have a nice spring to them.” After over a year of nearly daily use from two school-age kids (and their friends), her Neptune still looks pristine.

To make the best use of the Neptune’s full-size sleeper-sofa configuration, Alpert recommends springing for the brand’s Sleep Kit ($270), which includes a topper, fitted sheet, flat sheet, two pillows and pillowcases, and a comforter. All of this fits in the three storage compartments within the seat cushions, a “saving grace” in a house with linens galore, says Alpert.

This rounded-edge, injected-foam modular sofa—affectionally nicknamed “Chiclet”—epitomizes simplicity. It’s the ideal couch if you can’t stand saggy cushions or a wrinkly back. The re-launch of the original 1976 style from Herman Miller sofa designer Ray Wilkes preserves the postmodern splendor of the first edition, but offers new fabrics and colorways, including sunny recycled wool twill and textural viscose-wool bouclé in earthy palettes. Consider this iconic sofa more of an art form than just a place to sit, even if you can build out the two-seat into a spacious six-seat perch.

No need to agonize over whether you’re a left-chaise or a right-chaise person. This reversible design lets you change your mind. Slipcovered cushions provide a relaxed, lived-in look, while its compact footprint—set on a frame made from wood certified by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) to be responsibly sourced—makes it an especially smart pick for apartments, condos, and cozy living rooms. The modules allow you to adjust from a three-piece sectional to a sprawling, six-piece L-shape that can host a party.

Go ahead and dramatically drop down on the Lena sofa; the armless design will keep you from awkwardly hitting the arms. This showstopper from Sarah Sherman Samuel, with artful beam legs and a foam-seat construction, allows for just enough bounce. And because the streamlined silhouette has no sharp corners, you can sit two pieces next to each other for a glorious extended bench seating suited for a large living room.

As seen in Broadway actress Barrett Wilbert Weed’s Brooklyn Heights home, Arhaus is known for statement furnishings, and the Coburn fits the bill for plush lounging in style. Its 22-inch seat depth and down-and-feather–blend cushion fill combine to create a nest that is the ultimate definition of cozy. It’s also a top pick for a family with pets or kids because it comes upholstered in Crypton, an ultra durable fabric that can withstand spills, stains, and snags.

With seven distinct seat pieces, more than 140 upholstery options, and four leg covers, this Serena & Lily sectional wins the customization game. Incorporating the new addition to the Norfolk family, a curved corner piece with a 28-inch seat, creates a sectional with a sleek silhouette worthy of a lounge, especially when you accent the setup with a well-endowed arm chair. Layer on a few throw pillows to create an illusion of a cozy pit for hibernating over the weekend.

The modular design of the Article Beta sectional can work for 13 different configurations, including a love seat chaise and an L-shaped sofa with a chaise. Your living room is truly a canvas to experiment with this sectional, upholstered in a durable blend of polyester, viscose, linen, and cotton that makes it perfect for hosting. While the Beta only comes in three colors—white, cypress green, and gray—you can easily dress it up with a woven throw or a cuddle blanket.

Which Brands Offer the Most Versatile Configurations for Modular Sofas?

Serena & Lily and and Castlery stand out in this respect for offering design-forward options in performance fabrics. Article notably offers many configurations and deep seats.

Are Luxury Modulars Pet- and Kid-Friendly?

Depending on the fabric in question, plenty of modular sectionals are pet- and kid-friendly. Performance fabrics are as kid- and pet-friendly as it gets, designed to be durable, stain-resistant, and easy to clean. Luxury leather sectionals can be less pet- or kid-friendly than those upholstered in performance fabrics, as leather is no match for pet nails, for example. Arhaus notably offers modular sectional styles upholstered in Crypton, which allows liquids to roll off, not penetrate into the seat. The material is also designed to prevent scents from seeping in, making it a go-to for a pet family.

#4803. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4802. tk Best Ergonomic Office Chairs for a Stylish Workspace (2026)

There’s a reason I am most productive when working from an office, and it’s not the harsh lighting or lack of distractions: It’s my office chair. Previously, I was convinced that “ergonomic” was an empty buzzword used by chiropractors and human resources, but after working from a slew of supportive seats these last few years, I’m a believer. Ideally, office chairs combine a sophisticated aesthetic with a genuinely functional build—and both things can be true in the same design. Maybe that budget mesh chair you picked up from an office supply store does the job, but is it the right culture fit for the very curated aesthetic of your home? Fortunately, I’ve sourced the products that check all the boxes, because you deserve to feel just as productive in your guest room-slash-office space.

Over the years that the Shop AD team has been testing office chairs, often corralling the entire office to take a seat, we’ve expanded our search to curate a high-low selection that includes wallet-friendly picks, but also household names in the ergonomic space, like Herman Miller and Knoll. Our favorite options cosigned by design lovers—we are Architectural Digest after all—and those looking to cure that stubborn tech neck twinge, finally.

Our editors and writers have personally sat on, worked, and Zoomed from each of these picks, at the office and from their home desks. We can attest that not only are they attractive, but they will also provide structural support for your entire body, even through the longest meeting days and tightest deadlines.

As a general practice, the armrests on ergonomic office chairs tend to be bulky. Not so with the Branch Verve Chair, which stands out with its curvy S-shaped supports that give it some space-y, extraterrestrial appeal. The Verve is a newer and sportier model from the brand that set out to modernize dated office furniture (from standing desks to seating), and boasts a sleek breathable mesh back and some slender legs with casters for wheeling around the office.

Contributor Terri Williams notes that sitting for long periods of time is easy thanks to the V-shaped chair design that provides extra lumbar support. At just a hair shy of $600, this chair is also one of the most affordable picks on the list (so it’s a good fit for most people), and one of the most streamlined if you hate the look of typical corporate chairs. The svelte design is why we chose it as our top pick over the AD editor-beloved Ergonomic Chair Pro below, which might not be as visually appealing to the average person. “I can also adjust the height of the softly-padded armrests, the seat depth, the tilt, the tilt tension, and the padded lumbar support,” Williams says of the extra features here that put it into holy grail territory.

There’s a reason the Aeron is Herman Miller’s most beloved and recognizable office chair. The iconic design is truly supportive and customizable to fit your ideal comfort zones, with adjustable offerings from the armrests to the seat itself. The seat is almost bouncy, springing you upright and into the most ergonomic position possible. In her other office chair, shopping editor Audrey Lee sits on a cushion, but states that the Aeron balances support with real comfort. Contributor Zoë Sessums selected hers after a virtual fitting with an ergonomic expert at Herman Miller, who walked her through all the features. (Herman Miller offers an informative online gallery of both imagery and detailed videos if you’re unable to try out a chair in person.) Once the chair was delivered—no assembly required, it literally rolls out of the box—Sessums came away impressed with the power of the patented PostureFit SL back support, which encourages opening up the chest and shoulders, and tilts the pelvis slightly forward. “This chair will save your body,” she says. “It’s easy to see why people invest in supreme desk setups. I would recommend the Aeron chair again and again.”

A bad case of tech neck hates to see the Branch Ergo Pro coming. That’s because the chair’s fully customizable support system is calibrated to ensure that your posture is optimized, even during long hours in one fixed position. It offers 14 points of adjustments total (count ’em!) to keep you comfortable, from the seat height to the headrest for those who are blessed with longer limbs. And compared to the original version reviewed above, this one is far cushier on the seat and armrests, with seven additional points of adjustability. It is slightly less svelte and also slightly more expensive than its predecessor, the original Branch Ergonomic, which our tester Williams also loved for its ergonomic design.

Each of our editors took a spin on the Branch Ergo Pro (read our full review) and came away smitten with the adjustability points and glutes support of this “double-stuffed” chair. “I was especially fond of the arm rests that helped me achieve perfect elbow support with my laptop stand and that the adjustable tilt option gave me the freedom to stretch my back out whenever needed,” commerce editor Audrey Lee noted.

The only drawback is that the Ergo Pro needs assembly out of the box, and the construction process is a bit of a learning curve. Still, everything came together quickly in about 30 minutes or less and was easy enough to complete solo. Since it can be fully disassembled, it’s also a great option for frequent movers.

There’s a lot to like about Haworth’s Breck chair. Lee reported that it arrived swiftly in a large box that was simple to carry inside. The assembly won’t leave you frustrated either. You’ll find instructions on the flaps of the delivery box and Haworth has the same manual available on their website as well as a short video with step-by-step directions. The whole process literally takes less than a couple of minutes before you’re ready to put the chair in action.

Don’t be fooled by the easy assembly process, though, as this office chair is more advanced than meets the eye. “I first received the Breck during a heat wave and appreciated the ultra-breathable backrest which allowed a comfortable amount of air to flow through,” says Lee. But it’s all the adjustable features that stand out to her. Need more tilt? No problem. Wish the armrests were just a tad longer? Easy. Height? Seat depth? Lumbar support? Done, done, and done. And while these are all perks you would expect from a high-priced chair that costs over $1,000, the Breck supplies them at under $500.

A high price tag comes with great expectations—which the Asari chair met completely. Lee appreciated its attention to detail, which included the soft leather, the perfect amount of foam fill in the seat, and a backrest that makes it a treat to sit down and work. “The chair has noticeably softened in a delightful way that’s ultra-accommodating to my dimensions without feeling too sunken in or too stiff,” she says. Unlike leather executive office chairs that can read harsh or overly corporate, the Asari’s look is unparalleled. Lee “absolutely recommends” this chair to anyone looking to splurge on their home office. From physical appearance to practical use, it scores 10s across the board.

It’s rare for a truly ergonomic chair to look as good as the Herman Miller Management Chair does. I chose the brown checkerboard upholstery and stainless steel frame and, not to brag, but my coworkers have since declared FOMO, requesting fun office chairs of their own. Like most Herman Miller options, this chair is very adjustable—the features I focused on customizing to my liking were the seat height and the amount of recline the back can have (which is a lot, actually, I feel like I’m lying down if I push too hard). The back cushion has a bit more firmness to it than the ultra-plush seat cushion, which is great for posture correction and staying focused. While it’s a bit too soft for my all-day liking, I do appreciate the additional padding on days when I know I’ll be mostly stationary. I rarely need to adjust my position, and my knees never fall asleep, something that used to happen quite often in my too-tall office chair. Overall, the management chair is excellent for both a home and office environment. With over a dozen upholstery options, you won’t have to worry about the seat clashing with your existing decor—I find it a stylish midcentury alternative to the often all-black silhouettes that plague traditional offices.

For anyone in need of a custom office chair, Steelcase has solutions. Senior commerce editor Nashia Baker settled on this grey leather version from 23 upholstery options, which allow you to choose from peachy pinks, neutrals, and warm leather hues. The overall silhouette is narrower than most, but the armrests are adjustable and the seat has a soft, gentle glide when maneuvered up or down. Even the wheels are smooth when rolling over floors, carpet or tile. “This chair has literally made the trek with me across the Condé Nast office and on various floors, though I haven’t noticed the wheels wearing or jamming in the months I’ve been testing it,” Baker says. With its stable, upright backrest, the seat discourages slouching, but also has enough give for comfortably sitting hour after hour. At over $2,000, it’s definitely an investment, but for all the custom flourishes, Baker says it’s all worth it.

For those in search of a no frills office chair, this West Elm one is sleek and simple. This is the least adaptable option on this list, in that it doesn’t allow for any other heights or tilts. What it lacks in ergonomic adjustment points, however, it makes up for in design prowess. The sleek stainless steel frame and leather seat make a more eye-catching pair, while the true-ball wheels roll smoothly and without catching on the carpet in the AD office. This is definitely for those who prefer a firmer seat and I liked how upright this office chair felt, like it was almost correcting my posture while encouraging a better sense of productivity. My colleague, shopping editor Audrey Lee, however, wasn’t a fan, stating that it was too firm and didn’t love that the seat doesn’t swivel. “It’s a beautiful chair, and looks much more expensive than the price suggests,” Lee says. “It’s a divisive option, but the straightforward make is something I’d prefer to have at home, when all of my distractions are nearby, and I need the chair to do the heavy-lifting of forcing me to lock in.”

Branch’s Softside chair is a fully upholstered take on their more technical office chairs. It’s still as intuitively designed as the brand’s other chairs with its adjustment points (removable arms, adjustable height, and tension recline), two back heights, and caster wheels, but think of this as your at-home companion to the Ergonomic Pro. Brighter upholstery—I’m partial to the skylight blue—also helps to cheer up a workspace suffering from too much black and grey.

The iconic Danish brand HAY has made a number of noteworthy pieces, but we’re drawn to this amply cushioned roller chair. Dating back to 2009, the 155 Task Chair has two styles: standard and soft. The latter has foam padding and batting that keeps you supported through hours-long meetings. At 20 pounds, it’s a relatively lightweight item, and it conveniently arrives fully assembled for a fuss-free setup process. Plus, the curved seat is one of several ergonomic elements. The chair has a tilting mechanism and gas lift to adjust the angle and height of the seat. This is one of many chairs in HAY’s best-selling About a Chair collection, developed by award-winning furniture designer Hee Welling.

Introduced in 2021, the Zeph Chair is a collaboration between Herman Miller and Berlin-based design firm Studio 7.5. It also went on to earn one of AD’s 2022 Cleverest Awards, with editors noting its midcentury-modern design and ergonomic form for lower back support. The kinematic mono-shell is the most striking feature, a contoured seat and back with voids for a futuristic look. “Even better, the playful chair’s seat is made of 50% post-consumer recycled content and zero fabric waste,” adds Sessums. If you anticipate spending hours upon hours in this chair, we recommend the optional seat pad and arm rests for added comfort. Another thing to feel good about? The polymer shell is easy to clean with a damp cloth, and the 12-year warranty gives you extra peace of mind about investing in a relatively splurge-y item.

Louisa Pierce and Emily Ward of AD100 firm Pierce & Ward have been trusted to design homes for celebrity clients like Dakota Johnson and Emma Roberts, and their collaboration with West Elm shows their vintage-inspired, quiet luxury aesthetic. This button-tufted, swiveling office chair will instantly ground your space. It’s sophisticated and substantial, and the adjustable height lever is located under the seat. If the in-stock upholstery isn’t for you, there are 74 options to customize your chair. So, if you’re working from your living room or the office, you should feel right at home—a concept Pierce and Ward considered while designing their firm’s new Los Angeles studio. As Ward previously shared with AD, “There’s just a different kind of energy when a workspace feels like a home.” Keep in mind this is a limited-edition product, so it’s best to nab it ASAP.

One of the newest models from Swiss furniture manufacturer Vitra, the Mynt Task Chair is a thoughtfully designed, minimalist option for a modern office. Because of the slim profile, this would work well in a home office with a versatile, space-saving desk like the Pierce Wall Desk from West Elm. The natural oak veneer backrest, armrest, and seat is our preferred colorway, but the upholstered styles provide more cushioning, thanks to the polyurethane foam and polyester fiber fill. The responsive design adjusts the seat based on your movements (a.k.a. no manual adjustments needed), and the patented tilt mechanism is hidden within the aluminum frame. Pair it with an oak-stained desk to complement your chair, while also bringing more natural texture to a home office setup.

For the midcentury aesthetes, Arhaus’s leather pieces are contemporary takes on nostalgic silhouettes. Case in point: the Kirsten Faux Leather Desk Chair, an ergonomic approach to a classic leather seat, complete with rounded edges. It can easily find a home in an earth-toned office with a walnut-stained desk, and the antique brass legs add another natural hue to the design. And while it may look like it hails from a different era, there are plenty of updated features, such as the hydraulic lift to change up the height of the seat. Four sturdy, powdercoated aluminum legs are designed to endure long days at the office. And if you’re drawn to the shape of curved back and seat, the brand’s Kirsten collection includes dining chairs and stools. We like the faux leather upholstery, but Arhaus also makes this office chair with green performance velvet and white textured performance weave if you want try other options.

Our commitment to bringing you quality seat recs is well documented, and finding an office chair that is comfortable, well-made, and easy on the eyes can make a world of difference in how you feel while you’re sitting in a seemingly endless one-hour meeting. The Shop AD team thoroughly vets items before including them in our roundups, and we test nearly everything we write about—office chairs being no exception. I, alongside our broader team of writers and editors, tested more than 30 chairs combined to pull together these rankings, with only a few making the cut in our best-of list. I’ve yet to find a stylish, non-bulky gaming chair that meets our standard, and several other generic Amazon picks just didn’t feel elevated enough to make our list of chairs that would suit a design lover—though they may tick the boxes from a purely practical standpoint. Our reviews are always thorough, in-depth, and honest, even when we’re noting how a chair may have fallen short.

Weary workers can rest assured that every pick on this list has been hand-picked and personally vetted by us. Our well-rounded list includes design head-approved picks (Herman Miller! Knoll! Steelcase!) with more approachable best-sellers on Amazon (like Branch) sprinkled in, with top priority going to picks that had a warranty of at least seven years and merged great design with adjustability and comfort.

Over the years spent testing, we’ve also delisted picks from Article, Haworth, Herman Miller, Flash Furniture, Steelcase, Flexispot, and Humanscale that either felt not ergonomic enough for an office setting or didn’t feel like the most superlative choice for their price bracket compared to their peers. The Article Svelti is armless, for example, while the Steelcase Gesture had a stiff backrest and a tedious assembly process. An older version of the Branch Ergonomic has been replaced with the brand new Branch Ergonomic Pro, which was tested by several of our editors.

Whether from the desks of the Condé Nast offices or from home setups, the Architectural Digest team has spent weeks (sometimes months or years) sitting in, working from, and recording their thoughts on the best office chairs. I am a firm believer that the chair makes the workplace, and my fellow editors agree, assuring that each of these chairs met a specific set of criteria—which I’ve outlined below—in order to pass the qualifications to be included in this article.

Delivery and assembly: Straight out the gate, did the chair arrive within the guaranteed delivery window? And if you had to assemble it, was it relatively easy to do so or did it come with a tough-to-parse manual and 100 parts?

Dimensions: Apartment dwellers know better than anyone that being conservative with floor real estate isn’t a want, but a need. That’s why our reviews provide exact measurements for the styles we tested and any notes on whether we thought a chair might not be a good fit (literally) for a modest-sized workspace.

Rating the experience: A chair that’s both easy on the eyes and on the tush is our number one priority. What was your first impression of the chair? Does the design fit a clear aesthetic? Is it meant to be ergonomic? How do the materials perform, and do they seem durable? How did you feel after a full work day and week? Does it include any fun details that may not be obvious at first glance? Our reviews were crafted to give insight on why a chair could be the right one for your 40-hour work week.

What to keep in mind: Everyone has different ideas of perfection—which is why each chair also has a section detailing what a potential buyer should keep in mind. For example, if assembly was particularly difficult, if the chair had special care instructions, and if the design seemed polarizing, we made note of all that.

Editor’s Note: We recently de-listed the Article Svelti office chair due to it being armless in favor of more supportive options.

What Features Should I Look for in an Office Chair?

Our experts—TikTok’s favorite neurosurgeon, Betsy Grunch, MD, FAANS, FACS and Gainesville Physical Therapy's Kristy Basinger PT, CHT—agree that your back rest should be made from breathable material such as mesh for better air circulation, decreased perspiration, and greater comfort overall. Your seat is another important component for gluteal support that should have adequate padding consisting of dense foam or similar materials. Adjustability for different body types is crucial no matter which new chair you choose, so you can ensure your feet are positioned flat on the floor and arms set at a 90-degree angle.

Like any investment piece of furniture, you get what you pay for. There’s a lot of science that goes into crafting a comfortable and supportive office chair that you can actually be productive in. Ergonomic design, smooth movement, textiles, and manufacturing costs all combine to set the price point. Office chairs are so expensive because you’re not only investing in a chair, but also making an investment in your physical health. We spend at least eight hours a day in these seats, and they can dramatically affect our posture, joint health, and mobility. You may not notice the benefits of a great office chair, but you’ll definitely remember your discomfort in a bad one. Of course, there are budget-friendly options, like the Haworth Breck chair that we tested, which comes in above $400.

How Long do Office Chairs Typically Last?

High-quality office chairs typically last between seven and 10 years, which is why we prioritized picks that offer a lengthy warranty to cover the majority of this period. Cheaper office chairs have a much shorter lifespan, typically just a few years. Non-performance fabrics and leather seats will show their age more than performance materials that are better equipped to handle stains, scratches, and general wear and tear. You’ll know it’s time for a new seat when the customizable features—such as armrests, height, and seat position—start to wear out and aren’t as easy to adjust.

What Are the Differences Between Office Chair Styles?

Task: As the name suggests, task chairs are designed for specific tasks. Think of these chairs as short-term, minimal seating for quick bursts of work. They often have a less padded, simpler design and less support than true ergonomic office chairs that are designed for full days. Branch describes these seats as, “Task chairs embrace simplicity in their design, often characterized by a streamlined appearance. They prioritize functionality over excess features, aiming to deliver a no-frills seating solution that's easy to maneuver and adjust.” In this list, the Fritz Hansen Series 7 chair is a high-design task chair.

Executive: An executive office chair typically features a plush seat, high back, and ample spine support to keep you comfortable throughout the entire workday. You’ll find that these chairs offer more adjustment points and customization, like the 14 points on the Branch Ergonomic Pro we tested. Executive chairs come in a variety of materials and silhouettes, from Herman Miller’s signature Eames Aluminum Group chair to the brand’s more futuristic Aeron chair.

Gaming: The most specific type of office chair, gaming chairs have a very distinct shape. Usually with wide shoulders and an ultra-high back that supports your head and neck, gaming chairs prioritize lounge-style comfort without sacrificing ergonomic support. Most include a neck pillow and a lumbar pillow for additional padding and support. While the back is not as adjustable as some office chairs, gaming chairs offer additional customization points on the armrests and base.

Your office chair is just a piece of the puzzle when it comes to outfitting your WFH setup. Brands like Herman Miller, Steelcase, and Branch all offer great desks, filing cabinets, and bookcases to help fill your workspace with design-minded pieces. For those who value flexibility and ergonomic support, look to Branch for our top-tested seats and sit-to-stand desks that can withstand all-day, everyday use. For the midcentury obsessed, there’s no better place to find retro pieces than Design Within Reach. Essential brands like Eames, Knoll, and Vipp are all featured alongside some more modern favorites like Audo Copenhagen, HAY, and Tom Dixon. While we may not be able to channel the Scandinavian vacation policies, we can infuse our workspaces with more of their colorful minimalism to combat that three o’clock slump. For a full rundown of where to buy office furniture, read our guide here.

Across our vast library of home tours, we’ve noticed a few recurring characters for home offices that designers reach for again and again. Herman Miller, a favorite of our team as well, appears countless times. The retailer, having reached midcentury-modern icon status, is almost instantly recognizable. The aluminum frames, channeled leather upholstery, and wooden details elevate a home office while still providing tested ergonomic support. Jeff Goldblum’s California home boasts the brand’s Eames Aluminum Group chair, and Kevin Hart’s West Hollywood office features the Eames Executive Chair. Design Within Reach is another retailer designers frequent. Other midcentury staples can be found here too, like Knoll’s Morrison chair, the Vipp453+ Swivel Chair (which we’ve previously tested, but removed in favor of office chairs with more ergonomic features), and the Saarinen swivel chair (as seen in Margot Robbie’s production offices).

Does My Office Chair Need Lumbar Support?

Whether you’re sitting in your office chair eight hours a day or just here and there, yes, you need lumbar support. We’re all familiar with the aches that come when sleeping on a sofa for the night or after a long-haul flight, and proper back support helps to mitigate that pain and protect your spine in the process. According to our experts (Betsy Grunch, MD, FAANS, FACS and Gainesville Physical Therapy's Kristy Basinger PT, CHT, cited above), a proper-fitting desk chair is one of the cornerstones of postural health. People who sit for long hours in a poorly adjusted chair will experience neck, back, shoulder, and hip pain. This can trigger headaches, lack of concentration, and compression of the discs in the spine. Low back pain is one of the main reasons for missed days at work, so it’s essential to choose a chair that supports the spine. (It’s also not a bad idea to support your overall health and quality rest with a good mattress for back pain.)

#4797. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4793. Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 11:16 AM EST

What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your new favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”

You might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered issue, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

So when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

The options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.)

The solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

Harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

These days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

Because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

If you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

Opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

Maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

The idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he said, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

Unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.)

In the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

George Papanicolaou moved to New York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

His wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”

In 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

It took Stockard’s death, a new boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.

#4791. Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 12:05 PM EST

While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took issue with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered new approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”

“I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup said in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”

It took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”

Instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen said this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

“This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

But does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” said Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”

Okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he said. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”

#4790. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4787. First albatross egg of the season spotted at Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 2:03 PM EST

Nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

Black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

One special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

Wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

#4785. South Korea will use emergency alert system to warn about exam cheaters

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 3:10 PM EST

On Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with new tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

The sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han says he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student said in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place new anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin quickly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never said he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

While fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be new concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an important role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.
