#4783. 10 Best Sectional Sofas That Are Actually Stylish, Tested (2026)

As former AD editor Benjamin Reynaert puts it, sectionals allow for “a level of customization akin to bespoke furniture, but without the high costs that come with building a piece from the ground—or sofa leg—up.” Sectionals, more than standard sofas, have a kind of chameleonic style that can adapt just as easily to a basement movie room or the family den. But deciding between the right sectional versus a regular old sofa can still be tough.

If you’re worried that sectionals can lean a bit stodgy or will have trouble squeezing into tight spaces, we’re here to ease your mind with some of our team’s first-hand findings from years of sitting, napping, and binge-watching on the best sectional sofas around. Whether you’re looking for a chaise to stretch out on or a corner piece to anchor your media room, there’s a versatile silhouette just waiting to be brought home. Shop our favorite plush, sculptural picks and sleek, midcentury classics below.

Benchmade doesn’t stop at sending fabric swatches. The company will send you a true-to-size printouts so you know exactly what you’re getting, among more than 125 material and fabric combos of your choosing. That way, you can go beyond visualizing how the Modern Vintage sofa will fit in your space. The brand’s recently launched Vintage collection is for those of us who pine for retro designs but don’t want to spend the hours thumbing through Facebook Marketplace for a secondhand option. The line offers midcentury modern-inspired designs in patterned prints from the likes of Kravet and textile house Pollack. Contributor Noah Kaufman chose the plaid upholstery seen here from Pollack (which is available later this month) and a silhouette with sled legs to fit with his Victorian home’s aesthetic. “In a home with a more midcentury aesthetic, or one that uses more pronounced colors and patterns, it would fit right in,” Kaufman says, noting that the sofa reminds him of the couch in his childhood home.

Despite being known for budget-friendly bamboo and breezy linen bedding, Quince’s recent foray into furniture met our team with equal parts enthusiasm and curiosity. Handmade in North Carolina, where some of the best American furniture hails from, the pieces are designed to be home staples with a timeless aesthetic and for those who aren’t willing to shell out five figures for a sectional. After years spent with a well-loved, second-hand grey sofa, audience development manager Emma Tubbs knew it was time for an upgrade. Enter: Quince’s modern silhouette, the Ashford Deep Seat Chaise Sectional in the performance velvet. “When I found this Quince piece, I was immediately drawn to the gorgeous, deep brown velvet, but the deep seat is really what sold me,” she says. “I love being able to cozy up and lie down on a couch, and in my opinion, there's nothing worse than a narrow sectional.” With a 28-inch seat depth and cushions filled with high-density foam and a feather/down blend, this sofa is meant for all-day comfort. Her one critique: Tubbs notes that while the seat is supportive and plush, the back cushions easily lose their shape and need fluffing after every nap. That said, “the overall construction feels solid and well-made, and I’ve already taken many naps on the couch and woken up refreshed and without any back pain,” she says.

Velvet isn’t always the right upholstery choice for those looking for durability, but the brand’s performance velvet easily withstands spills and pets, needing just a spot clean when you notice a stain. Overall, Tubbs notes that it’s great for game nights just as it is for sick days and rainy weekends spent reading indoors. Even her dog gives it the thumbs up: “While we’re trying to limit our 80-pound very hairy German Shepherd’s access to the new couch, it does warm my heart that the couch can comfortably accommodate all three of us sprawled out.”

Castlery’s Hamilton sectional has a classic design with its tapered arms and boxy shape, and it also happens to be a sleeper sofa. Suiting a more modern or traditional aesthetic, the sectional keeps its structure while still being a crazy comfortable place to lounge around. “My partner and I are true couch people and love to lie around, so getting another sectional was the obvious choice,” says contributor Susie Plotkin. Plotkin goes on to describe this couch as wildly comfortable, and having the kind of silhouette that makes her living room look more polished than it is. It won’t be your living room’s signature piece of decor, but for those looking for a sectional that can easily adapt to their ever-evolving design style, the Hamilton might be for you.

The perk of having a sleeper sofa and a sectional in one is that there is plenty of room to spread out. And for those short on closet space, the chaise lifts up to reveal a storage compartment underneath. But unlike other jack-of-all-trades furniture pieces, this one delivers in just two boxes. Plotkin opted for white-glove delivery, and the entire couch was assembled and ready for a movie night in under an hour.

Like most sleepers, the built-in, memory foam mattress may not compare to your plush bed setup, but Plotkin insists that guests have touted the Hamilton’s comfort, night after night. “We’ve already had people sleep on both the pull-out mattress and directly on the chaise; both got glowing reviews,” she says. “The middle seat is a hair stiffer than the others because of the pullout mattress, but even that is very lounge-able. It feels well-made and durable, and because the high-density memory foam cushions retain their shape, the couch doesn’t sag.” Overall, Plotkin is extremely pleased with her sectional, especially the way it's held up against her two very rambunctious kittens (and their claws). The performance upholstery is stain-resistant and has a subtle texture that adds depth to the otherwise all-white look. Since she doesn’t have a guest room, she was looking for a versatile piece—“not just any sleeper sofa, though, a seating unicorn: a stylish, comfortable, non-bulky sleeper sectional” for her space. “It didn’t even occur to me to look for storage—I was already being greedy with my requirements, so when I found the Hamilton, it skyrocketed to the top of the shortlist,” Plotkin adds.

The Burrow is a family-friendly addition to your living spaces no matter what kind of square footage you’re working with. This three-piece sectional that’s just slightly larger than a loveseat is especially accommodating for smaller layouts and thoughtfully designed with the flexibility to tack on more seating (an ottoman, chaise, or extension here or there) as your family or space changes. The sofa’s stain-resistant upholstery, solid plywood frame, and CertiPUR-US–certified foam base also ensures lasting durability and high-quality comfort. The brand also offers a one-year warranty to give you a bit more peace of mind.

Contributor David Kaufman placed it an entryway area of his home and called it “a great starter sofa for a first home or apartment that you won’t have to send to a landfill when you’re ready to move.” He noted that it falls on the firmer end, but vouches that it’s still a comfy crowd-pleaser among the family. “It’s especially well sized for the twins to curl up in with a friend.”

The Arhaus Coburn reclining sectional is a blocky, yet modernized option (we love the exaggerated seams) for anyone looking for a comfortable recliner that’s trimmed of all the bulk of the Lay-Z-Boys from the early aughts. “The couch is exceptionally comfortable and plush, especially when you use the reclining feature,” says AD contributor Blake Bakkila, who cautions that when you’re not using it in recliner mode, it doesn’t provide as much shoulder or neck support. Another perk of the sofa is its kid-friendly surface, put to the test by Bakkila’s toddler. “The kitchen (and his beloved berries) are a quick sprint from the couch, and we’ve never noticed any stains,” Bakkila adds. It does need ample inches of clearance at the back in order to recline, so it would be better suited for floating furniture layouts rather than a room where it would need to be placed against a wall. Note that this sofa also needs to be plugged into a power source or equipped with battery packs to use the reclining features.

Thuma made a name for themselves with easy-to-build bed frames which lock into place via well-crafted Japanese joinery, though they quickly followed that up with bedroom furniture like nightstands and other modular shelving arrangements. Their most recent launches have positioned Thuma as a brand to know for beautiful furnishings in every room of the house, starting with their new modular sofas. Enhanced with additional lumber support and enforced with liquid-coated steel, these pieces are sturdy and also elegant, with commerce partnerships manager Evan Russum giving them top marks for style and design alone.

“This couch stood out to me because it avoids the bulky, overstuffed look a lot of sectionals lean into,” Russum says. “Instead, it feels streamlined and modern, with modular pieces that clip together in a seamless way that echoes the bed frame’s design ethos.” He noted that there is plenty of room to sprawl out for his lanky 6’5 frame and that despite its delicate ivory color, the couch hasn’t seen any scratches from his cat, snags, or noticeable wear from daily use.

Interior Define’s Sloan sectional offers more customization options than the traditional furniture brand. Choose from dozens of upholstery materials (and colors!), various seat depths, cushion fills, and even leg styles. The personalization is largely why contributor Malia Griggs chose this sofa for her living room. “I really do love this couch. If you enjoy tailoring your décor to your taste, are willing to pay a bit more for quality, and have the patience for a made-to-order process, this is a wonderful sectional—especially for a smaller space (and even with cats),” she says. Having stretched out on the chaise for movie nights, naps, and even one full night, Griggs touts the sofa’s firm yet cozy seat and durable upholstery.

Even with two rambunctious cats, the sofa has held up against spills, stains, claws, and even one poorly timed hairball. “The sectional has held up surprisingly well against their havoc—wrestling on the chaise, treating its sides like a scratching post, and near-constant shedding absolutely everywhere,” Griggs elaborates. She also says that a soft-bristle brush helps maintain the velvet texture and disguises any aggressively clawed areas. “While I wouldn’t call velvet a low-maintenance upholstery choice (it definitely attracts lint and pet hair), it has performed better than I expected,” she says. “Velvet has a short, dense pile that doesn’t snag the same way as my previous chenille sofa—so even when my cats do go to town with their claws, the fabric doesn’t show damage as obviously.”

“We were inspired to create 7th Avenue to solve for a frustration we kept hearing from customers: Finding a sofa that was both beautifully designed and genuinely practical for everyday living was surprisingly difficult,” the brand’s co-founder and CEO Billy Shaw previously told AD. The result is ultra-modular pieces like this chaise sectional, complete with water-repellent and stain-resistant fabric upholstery that are removable and washable (and replaceable if you ever want to mix it up).

Similar to the chaise sectional, this sectional sofa from 7th Avenue promises modularity and water-resistant and stain-repellent properties. The construction is modular, of course, but contributor Meg Kernahan explains how the overall look can coordinate with virtually any interior design. “This sectional has a very versatile look that can work with many different styles,” she shares in her review. “The sleek, no-frills design makes it a perfect backdrop for other elements in the room to stand out. My style leans organic modern with a touch of midcentury, and it blends with my aesthetic well.” Kernahan selected a chocolate brown color, in the hopes that the dark hue and stain-resistant fabric could conceal any marks left behind by her two young kids and dog. She notes that while it’s not completely water-resistant, it can easily repel a splash of water, and that it’s easy to remove the cushion covers and throw them in the wash.

Kernahan calls this couch “incredibly comfy” and says her family has taken several naps on it. “My husband and I can each lie down on either side of the couch at the same time without having to drape our legs over each other (we’re both about 5' 8"), so there is plenty of room to sprawl out and get comfortable,” she says. “It’s notably deep enough for a full night’s sleep (or a solid nap), especially with the back cushions removed.” And after a month of testing (and sleeping) on it, she hasn’t noticed any sagging.

Comfort and natural materials are top priorities for Sixpenny, which rebranded in 2020 to develop eco-friendly pieces with slipcover upholstery. Their feather down is ethically sourced, and the down alternative fill is made with vegan poly fibers. Our team has tested dozens of sectionals, but contributor Zoë Sessums argues this might be the comfiest she’s ever tried. “You can really sink into the seats, yet the cushion filling bounces right back,” she writes in her review. “It feels durable and well made, especially all the stitching on the slipcovers.”

Two years after bringing it home, Sessums says “all the cushions still have so much oomph” and continue to feel supportive—even after cats, dogs, small children, and tall overnight guests have all comfortably used this couch, without causing any damage. “This sofa feels nearly indestructible!” Sessums adds. Even more, her guests often ask if she purchased a new couch because she’s rearranged the units to create different configurations over the years. “Currently, I have the sofa set up as a small sofa and two chairs,” she says. “It’s a nice way to refresh your space while being less wasteful. I sometimes wish the depth was slightly shorter since my house isn’t very big, but overall it works.”

Pottery Barn has been a trusted source for high-quality furniture for decades, so it’s no wonder they make one of the most comfortable—and dare we say “dreamiest”—sectionals. “The level of comfort that this couch possesses is the stuff of legend,” writes contributor Jaha Nailah Avery in her review. “It’s probably the most comfortable couch I have ever had the pleasure of sitting on. It’s constructed so well, and you can definitely tell that it’s made from premium materials.”

True to its name, the Dream is a standard product with several customizations: two widths, an optional storage ottoman, and 80 colorways to choose from. Avery selected the wider version, and says it fits perfectly in her single-family home with a large living room. “At 172 inches wide, 86 inches deep, and 34 inches high, it is quite long, but it fills the space in a way that makes everything a little more cozy,” she explains. “I also love that you can customize its size. You can pop out one or two of the middle sections to make it smaller, or move the ottoman piece to another section.” Her dog Fievel gives a rave review, too, since the upholstery is gentle on his sensitive skin and easy to vacuum or lint roll his hair.

There are many factors we considered in each of our reviews to give you the insight you need to select the best sectional sofa for your home, including:

Ordering and customization process: Shallow seats or deep seats, armrests or armless, right-facing chaise or left-facing chaise, down seat cushions or foam cushioning, upholstery or leather, L-shape or U-shape—each of the sectionals we tested has possibilities. We also documented the lead times and expected delivery timelines for each model.

Couch delivery and assembly: Curbside or white-glove, fully assembled or DIY. And, if DIY, how many pieces did the sofa arrive in and how difficult was the assembly?

After installation: Here we asked some tough functionality questions of each sectional: Is it practical for a modern home? Is the couch kid- and/or pet-friendly? What are the care and cleaning instructions? And did it look better IRL than in the photos?

Durability and longevity: When possible, we followed up with testers to see if they still stood by their original reviews months or years down the line.

We updated this story for Seat Week 2025 with couches that AD staffers and contributors spent the summer vetting, including a new reclining sofa. Above all else, we prioritized picks during testing that were stylish, comfortable, reasonably easy to assemble, and durable enough not to stain or tear even when pets and children are present. Only picks that earned at least a B grade in our testing (which was appointed according to the factors outlined above) made the cut. Over the last successive updates, we’ve delisted picks from Lovesac and Sundays that felt less elevated than their peers for the price point. Meanwhile, a best-selling style from Albany Park that we tested has been retired by the brand as of 2026.

Of course, our homes and apartments can only fit so much seating, so we added a section of runner-up styles that we hope will round out your search for a beautiful, comfortable sofa, no matter what your budget may be. We haven’t tested these models firsthand, but we made sure to choose design-forward styles that are sold at reliable retailers. Most even include customer reviews that offer a glimpse at how these sectionals would hold up in your own home.

Deciding what sectional shape you’re in the market for will help you streamline your decision making. Take into account exactly how much square footage you have to fill, along with what kind of space it will occupy (a family-friendly space with lots of foot traffic will require different kinds of materials than a rarely used guest room, for example).

L-Shaped Sectional: Arguably the most traditional sectional shape, and the one you’ll come across most on this list, L-shaped sectionals are suitable for just about any space. They’re space maximizers—snugly fitting into corner areas and making the most out of your square footage. They also create a shape that can be corralled around a few accent chairs or a statement-making armchair (something like an Eames lounger). If you’re looking for styling inspiration, we’d point you in the direction of this Parisian apartment which coordinates the sectional and wall color to create the illusion of a bigger room, or this Gramercy Park apartment where a sectional sits back in an otherwise open layout.

U-Shaped Sectional: U-shaped sectionals are ideal for larger families looking for lots of seating as well as the perpetual hosts and hostesses, who want party guests to have a spot to kick back. For true U-shape inspiration, look to Stacey Bendet’s Upper West Side abode, where a green velvet U-shape sectional serves as the centerpiece in the designer’s colorful living room.

Curved Sectional: A cousin of the L-shaped and U-shaped sectional, the curved sectional isn’t bound by static lines. At times it takes on a true "U" design, while we’ve also seen configurations take on a snake-like S-shape. Like an L-shaped sectional, some curved sectionals work nicely in corner spots like this one in Pierre Yovanovitch’s Paris office. Curved sofas and sectionals are also unique because they don't necessarily feel out of place in the center of a room, whereas a more angular couch may create an awkward flow. If you think this type of sectional might be your vibe, we'd use the curvaceous seating arrangements in Chrissy Teigen and John Legend's home designed by AD100 designer Jake Arnold as your style inspiration.

Modular Sectional: We consider modular sectionals to be the jack-of-all-trades of the seating world. With a modular arrangement the world is your oyster—want to add more seating to your L-shaped sectional by making it into a U? No problem. Not happy with a sectional all together? Lots of modular designs actually allow you to re-configure your furniture into single and loveseats. Think: Colman Domingo’s impressive Ligne Roset Togo configuration or the Mario Bellini velvet number in this Los Feliz home.

Sofa With Chaise: If you’re not completely sold on the idea of a sectional, a sofa chaise is the perfect middle ground. With this option, there’s no need to agonize over whether a left or right facing chaise works with your space—the detachable chaise allows you to switch it up.

What Features Should I Look for in the Best Sectional Sofas?

Determining the right size sectional for your space is key to a) getting it in the door and b) ensuring that the arrangement doesn’t overwhelm your living room. We would classify three size categories to help you narrow down which to make shopping a little easier on you:

Seat depth—or the distance between the backrest and the outer edge of the seat cushion—is another factor that you’ll want to consider for the ultimate comfort to match your height. There’s no right seat depth, per se, but a deeper-seated sofa is better suited for someone leggier or simply sprawling out, while something more narrow is ideal if you’re looking to sit more upright. Brands like Interior Define also custom make sectionals to your exact depth preference if you have a specific number in mind.

While we’d all like to champion the white couch lifestyle, it’s not always practical if you’re sharing a home with little ones or pets. Thankfully advancements in upholstery tech have developed performance fabrics that promise resistance to spills and durability against everyday wear and tear. You could easily add a luxurious feel to your space with a jewel-toned velvet à la John Legend and Chrissy Teigen or Vanessa Hudgens. But if you’re a traditionalist, you might find inspiration from neutral picks like Ashley Tisdale’s Sixpenny or Taylor Hill’s cloud sofa.

Lately, designers are demonstrating that statement sectionals are something to aspire to. One look at Kendall Jenner’s “grandma-chic” chintz sofa upholstered in Lee Jofa’s Hollyhock Handblock print, under the guidance of AD100 designer Heidi Callier, is an invitation to expand your own floral dreams. (Open Door viewers wouldn’t stop praising the bold design choice.)

A recent report on designers’ couch trend predictions for 2026 are generally pointing to a shift from blocky silhouettes to styles with rounded edges (à la Mario Bellini’s infamous Camaleonda sofa). These bulbous styles owe a lot to the popularity of conversation pits, encouraging banter between seated guests and a comfy, closed-in feel. Postmodern, relaxed silhouettes like the Natuzzi and slouchy Maralunga profiles are also enduringly relevant as cool personas of the sofa world.

When it comes to colorful choices, florals, plaids, and stripes are offered more frequently as ready-to-ship. People are also overwhelmingly gravitating to 1970s colorways and styles that are laid-back and comfy. But unlike something you’d find in an old wood-paneled basement, the upholstery is often applied to modern silhouettes.

#4782. Fiona the hippo under 24-hour care after swallowing hat

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 3:54 PM EST

UPDATE, November 19, 2026, 4:15 p.m. EST: Fiona the hippo has died.

Fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

Last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

“Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”

The zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”

On Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

#4781. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4780. The Vuori and Baleaf Black Friday Leggings Deals We’re Shopping This Year

And which label gives you a better bang for your buck.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Black Friday is arguably the best time of year to stock up on activewear and athleisure—especially those pricier pieces you’ve been eyeing for months. And if your leggings drawer is due for a refresh, chances are you’ve perused styles from Vuori and Amazon favorite Baleaf. Both brands have amassed a loyal following for their comfy, functional activewear, albeit at very different price points. The good news? Black Friday deals make a new pair from either brand an even sweeter purchase.

As a style writer who’s spent years testing leggings, I’d steer those looking for buttery-soft fabrics and versatile styles that transition seamlessly from Pilates to lounging toward Vuori. Baleaf, on the other hand, excels at affordable, performance-driven leggings with practical features like roomy pockets and fleece-lined interiors for outdoor winter workouts. Ultimately, the better buy depends on how you plan to wear your leggings—which is why I’ve broken down the best Black Friday deals from both brands below.

Baleaf’s leggings are already a steal at full price, ringing in at less than half the cost of many Vuori styles. Throw in Black Friday discounts of 20 to 40% off, and you can stock up on multiple pairs without putting much of a dent in your wallet. We especially love Baleaf’s more workout-focused styles, from its fleece-lined leggings that make winter walks considerably more bearable to its workout tights with generously sized pockets and moisture-wicking fabric. The fabrics may not feel quite as luxe as Vuori’s, but in terms of functionality for the price, Baleaf is tough to beat.

#4779. Audiophiles are eating good this December with new headphones and earbuds from classic American brands

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 4:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

If you’re into personal audio, you might not want to spend all your money during Black Friday/Cyber Monday (but feel free to spend a little, and keep coming back here for some great suggestions as to how). Just within the last week, several innovative new headphones and earbuds have been announced, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

First up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the new Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

The 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously announced $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

Compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

Being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

As for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

Over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the company has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

The overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the company’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

To ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

#4777. Rare rhino birth caught on camera at England’s Chester Zoo

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 7:01 PM EST

On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage shows rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been announced yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

At birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

The team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help plan out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

“Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she showed signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos said in an e-mailed statement. “It was a big moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”

Both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

“Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”

While not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Currently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

While the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species currently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This new calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

“Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”

#4775. Where Does Caroline Kennedy Live Now? Unpacking the Former First Daughter’s Real Estate Portfolio

She entered the public eye as a little girl living in the White House, but where does Caroline Kennedy live now? The only surviving child of President John F. Kennedy and Jacqueline Kennedy, the diplomat and author has lived in many prominent homes throughout her life, the Executive Mansion being just one of them. Below, we’re unpacking all of the places that Caroline has called home.

An aerial view of the Kennedy Compound in Hyannisport, Massachusetts

In 1956, the year before Caroline was born, her parents paid $45,948 for a home at the Kennedy Compound in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, where JFK’s parents and brother, Robert F. Kennedy, also owned homes. The 4,500-square-foot residence was built in the mid-20s, which is also the period when the famed family first put roots in the area. Born on November 27, 1957, Caroline spent childhood summers at the Cape Cod enclave. It was also where, on July 19, 1986, she married museum exhibit designer Ed Schlossberg.

Caroline Kennedy and Edwin Schlossberg on their wedding day in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts

When Jacqueline died in 1994, the property went to Caroline and her brother, John F. Kennedy, Jr., but reportedly, only John spent his summers there. After he and his wife, Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, tragically died in a 1999 plane crash, the home’s ownership went to Caroline and her children. In 2004, Caroline sold the dwelling to her uncle, Senator Edward Kennedy, for $3 million. “It was sold to the senator to keep it in the family,” family friend Dick Gallagher told the Cape Cod Times. “It will always be the president’s house.”

Caroline spent her first few years primarily living in Washington, DC’s Georgetown neighborhood. In late 1957, her parents paid $82,000 for a brick Federal-style home and tapped designer Sister Parish to decorate its interiors. The Kennedys lived at the circa 1811 property, known as the William Marbury House for the Federalist financier who first lived there, until JFK’s 1961 presidential inauguration. John Jr. was also born during this period. The 5,215-square-foot residence was most recently sold in May 2026 for $6.125 million.

US President John F Kennedy in the Oval Office of the White House with John Kennedy Jr and Caroline Kennedy in 1962

Of course, the next residence that the Kennedys took up was the White House, where they lived from 1961 until President Kennedy’s 1963 assassination. Caroline attended kindergarten in the White House’s solarium along with about 20 other children. She was photographed riding her pony named Macaroni, a gift from Lyndon B. Johnson, on the White House lawn for Life magazine in 1962. The image inspired Neil Diamond to write his hit song, Sweet Caroline. In 2011, Caroline recalled celebrating childhood Halloweens in America’s most famous dwelling: “One of my favorite memories of living here is dressing up in my witch costume and going over to scare my father in his office,” she said.

After JFK’s death, Jacqueline, Caroline, and John moved back to Georgetown, in a $175,000 home known as the Newton D. Baker House, on the same street as their former home in the neighborhood. After less than a year of being hounded by tour buses at the residence, Jackie put the 1794-built Federal-style dwelling up for sale and headed for the Big Apple.

Jackie Kennedy Onassis outside of her 1040 Fifth Avenue home

The family of three moved into a 14-room penthouse apartment on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, which Jacqueline bought in July 1964 for $200,000. The 5,300-square-foot home had five bedrooms, five-and-a-half baths, and views of Central Park and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where Caroline later worked and met her future husband. The 18-story limestone building was built in 1930 by prominent architect Rosario Candela. The penthouse unit had a library, conservatory, three fireplaces, and a balcony overlooking the park. Caroline lived there until 1972, when she left to attend a boarding school in Massachusetts. Jacqueline called the apartment home until her 1994 death. A year later, billionaire David Koch bought the unit for $9.5 million.

An aerial view of Jackie Kennedy’s Martha’s Vineyard property

In 1979, Jacqueline bought Red Gate Farm, a 340-acre property on Martha’s Vineyard, for $1.1 million. At the time, only a small hunting cabin sat on the grounds. The former First Lady soon built an impressive compound comprised of a Cape Cod–style main house with five bedrooms, a four-bedroom guesthouse, a three-bedroom caretaker’s house, a boathouse, a storage building, two garages, a pool, a tennis court, and a treehouse for her grandchildren.

The property stayed in the family long after Jacqueline’s death. Caroline and Schlossberg’s daughter, Tatiana, was married at the residence in 2017. Two years later, Caroline listed Red Gate Farm for $65 million. “Forty years ago, my mother fell in love with Martha’s Vineyard. When she found Red Gate Farm, it was a perfect expression of her romantic and adventurous spirit,” she said in a statement. “The dunes and ponds and rolling hills of Aquinnah gave her the chance to create a world where she could be so close to nature, close to her family and friends, and, most importantly, close to her beloved books.”

In a letter printed in The Vineyard Gazette, Caroline explained her rationale for the sale. “Being able to raise our children in a place that meant so much to my mother and my brother has kept them close to our hearts. Now that our children are grown, it is time for them to spread their wings, and for us to explore new places.” The diplomat also recalled her pleasant memories at the property over the years: “Together we wove the traditions of summer across three generations — setting lobster pots in Menemsha Pond, entering the Fair and never winning, growing a vegetable garden, bringing home the best shell from the beach every day, getting stuck at the airport when the fog rolled in.”

In 2020, 304 acres of the property sold for $27 million to two nonprofits: the Martha’s Vineyard Land Bank Commission and the Sheriff’s Meadow Foundation. In 2025, it opened to the public as the Squibnocket Pond Reservation. A year later, the Land Bank Commission paid an additional $10 million for a 32-acre portion.

Caroline and Schlossberg still own 95 acres of the property, including the main house and guesthouse.

Caroline and Schlossberg primarily raised their children, Rose, Tatiana, and Jack, in an apartment on Park Avenue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. The dwelling has six rooms and was described in a 2009 NBC News report as “a low-key place covered with books and decorated with slip-covered sofas.” The couple seems to still own the residence.

Following Tatiana’s tragic death to cancer in June 2026, Jack told People that his parents had moved in with Tatiana’s husband to help take care of their grandchildren, aged two and four years old. “My parents are grandparents, but they’re really playing the role of new parents right now,” Jack told the outlet. “They live with my niece and nephew and take care of them every single day… they’re all living in the same apartment.” Three months before her death, Tatiana and her husband bought an Upper East Side co-op unit near her parents’ apartment.

#4772. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4771. 'I Kickstarted My Upper-Body Strength Transformation Using Only A 25-Lb. Bag Of Rice'

"I developed so much discipline that translated into every other aspect of my life."

As soon as I started walking, I was playing a sport. I don’t remember there being a time where I wasn't on a sports team during my childhood. To me, exercise was practice after school and traveling for games on the weekend for whatever sport I was playing. As a teen, in my off-seasons, my mom would beg me to go to the gym with her for fun, but I didn't have much interest in it.

I liked running and endurance-based activities because I felt like they complimented sports pretty well, especially lacrosse, which eventually became my main activity. I ended up being able to play lacrosse in college, where I was first required to start strength training to prepare for the season. While I was in shape for my sport, I couldn’t even lift the bar in the gym, and I was mesmerized by all the different movements that I didn’t really understand.

In the middle of college, everyone was sent home because of the pandemic. I felt far away from my entire life and all my friends, and like there was nothing for me to be doing. There was so much time on my hands, and there was nowhere for me to be.

While sitting at home alone, I had nothing to do besides work out. To pass the time and cope with what was happening, I wanted to exercise, but I felt stuck since gyms were closed.

Then my dad handed me this 25-pound bag of rice from Costco and said, “You can train with this. There’s actually a lot you can do with it.” So I stuffed that bag of rice in a backpack to make it heavy, and I’d use it as a weight. I would put the backpack at the front of my body and do squats. I would use it as a kettlebell for kettlebell swings. I would put it on my back and do walking lunges.

I realized there was a lot I could do at home, but I wanted to try to strength train at the actual gym. I decided that, when I was done playing college lacrosse, I would get serious about a gym routine.

When I graduated from college, I was excited—but so confused—about where to begin. I followed fitness influencers on TikTok who gave workout tips and advice on which movements to try. But I also wanted to make sure all of my information was accurate and science-based, so I started researching online, watching the moves other people at the gym were doing, and reaching out to my old college coaches for tips.

At first, I thought I needed to be running and lifting every day to stay fit, but I soon realized I was over-exerting my body. I started learning more about the basics of strength training and how to work different muscles with compound movements like squats, deadlifts, hang cleans, and more. I also learned how to supplement those movements by doing auxiliary exercises with dumbbells or body weight exercises like curls, lunges, and more.

After a combination of trial and error, researching, and practicing at the gym, I finally found my strength training routine and stride. I started to finally perfect my strength exercises. My confidence was growing so much as a result, which only motivated me to continue. I developed so much discipline that translated into every other aspect of my life.

Even when things got off-routine for me, I could fall back into strength training to find my rhythm again. I know it’ll always be there, giving me structure even when everything else feels unsettled.

When I first started lifting, I was hungrier because I was training more, but I was afraid to eat more. But if you want to build muscle, you need protein and you have to eat! It’s how your body survives and thrives. You need to take care of yourself, and that includes getting enough sleep.

I do not always feel motivated to workout. That’s just how life is. But when I started strength training, I developed so much discipline. Even when I don’t have motivation, that discipline is there now, not just at the gym. Stick with it and allow that habit to form.

It’s honestly true when they say that movement is medicine. When I'm taking care of my body, even if my mental headspace isn't in peak condition, I feel better after movement. It’s not all about hitting personal bests, either. (Though those certainly help!) I might tell myself, “I don't want to go to the gym today, but I will because I know it’s good for me.” Strength training gives me the confidence to know I can do anything I set my mind to.

Nowadays, I strength train four days a week, and I’ll also do a designated cardio day. I base my training on muscle groups.

Each workout will have a main exercise, such as a squat, bench press, or deadlift. Then, I pair them with auxiliary exercises like lunges, quad extensions, hamstring curls, rear delt flies, incline dumbbell bench presses, and more that target smaller muscles.

I try to stay between four to five exercises per workout so I don't overdo it. I like to keep it simple when I write my workout plans. I’ll follow those plans for a certain number of weeks depending on my goals, then I’ll move on from there. I like to keep things interesting for myself to ensure I never get bored, because I want to be able to do this forever.

I used to not be able to hang clean the bar, and once I even dropped it on my knee and ruptured my bursa. It was all bruised, and I was so embarrassed. From then on, I had a real mental block with hang cleans. I told myself, “I’m never going to be able to do a lot of weight.”

Years later, I decided it was about time I face my fear. I worked my way up to being able to put 25-pound plates on each side, coming out to about 100 pounds, depending on the bar. The more I practiced, the easier it became for me, and getting there was a huge milestone.

Any upper-body movements are especially empowering to me. Many people don’t think you can have impressive upper-body strength as a woman. When I was able to work my way up to putting a 45-pound weight on each side for bench presses, coming out to 135 pounds, I felt unstoppable. It was such a big deal to me since I never thought I’d be able to do it. It’s such an empowering feeling to be doing something that a lot of people see as something only men would do.

#4768. Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print says “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4767. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

Use your best judgment, but if you’re not totally confident on your cadence, ask your hairstylist.

More than 50 percent of women will experience some form of hair loss, according to the Cleveland Clinic—and taking action is easier than you think. Hair shedding can be caused by hormonal fluctuations, stress, dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis, and genetics (just to name a few). So, you’ll want to ask a dermatologist to get to the bottom of what's causing your thinning. However, getting your at-home routine down pat helps support a healthy scalp—and don’t just take my word for it. "There are certain basic properties of shampoo that can be hugely beneficial if you’re trying to prevent or reduce hair shedding,” says dermatologist and hair specialist James Kilgour, MD, in our guide to the best shampoos for thinning hair.

Pureology Hydrate Sheer Nourishing Shampoo

Shea Moisture Intensive Hydration Shampoo

All of these featured picks have been personally tested by our team of editors or earned snaps from dermatologists. Case in point: Deputy editor Carina Hsieh, MPH, used Ouai Fine Hair Shampoo daily and was genuinely impressed that her hair has way more volume and bounce throughout the day. “My hair has more lift at the roots—almost the way it used to, pre-30s,” she says in her review. “My bangs are banging again (physically, emotionally, and, of course, spiritually), and my hair no longer separates into the same three sad little strands it seemed to automatically separate into every 2 p.m.”

Dr. Kilgour also regularly uses Olaplex shampoo. He appreciates that the sulfate-free shampoo contains amodimethicone, a smoothing polymer that leaves his hair more manageable. "The bond-building ingredients are good for maintaining the strength and the health of the hair you have rather than making your hair look thinner—it has less of a role in stimulating new growth by itself," he says.

When I moved from Florida to New York, my scalp was easily irritated and my hair color faded quickly. I thought it was due to testing dozens of beauty products for work. However, after chatting with dermatologists in our guide to the best hard water shampoos, I realized that the hair-coating minerals in my shower pipes were to be blamed. In addition to using a shower head filter, I prioritized shampoos made with deep-cleaning ingredients, such as vitamin C, apple cider vinegar, and EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid). Shampoos with “buildup remover,” “clarifying,” or “chelating” on the label are helpful for removing minerals found in hard water.

Design Essentials Oat Protein and Henna Deep Cleansing Shampoo

These picks tick off all of these suggestions—and they earned snaps from dermatologists, trichologists, and hairstylists. I also tested a few and can vouch for their efficacy. Notably, Joico is my no-fail recommendation for hard water and after swimming in the ocean or pool. Meanwhile, Design Essentials gets the deep cleansing done without depleting my dry hair and scalp of its natural oils. Ouai Detox Shampoo earned snaps from dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD, because it contains apple cider vinegar (ACV) to help remove hard water, debris, and buildup.
